[SPEAKER_04]
Ladies and gentlemen, FCCI is pleased to welcome you to this Monday afternoon presentation from the Inspired to Lead Conference at the Ritz -Carlton Dove Mountain Resort in Tucson, Arizona. This afternoon's keynote speaker is the founder and managing partner of a growing early stage venture fund in Chicago, Illinois. With a strong desire to invest in founder -focused, redemptive purposes, our speaker has established an investment strategy that empowers founders, businesses, and ultimately cultures to reflect the profound and enduring truths of our faith. Speaking from his desire to motivate greater levels of commitment to leadership and family well -being, would you please join in welcoming to the Ritz -Carlton Ballroom stage a compelling voice for healthy founders building healthy companies? Mark Phillips.

[SPEAKER_00]
Wow, that was an awesome video. Ken told me that it was going to be good, but that was fantastic. It's such a pleasure to be here. Thank you for having me. The timing of this is perfect because I want to start our conversation talking about food, actually. Let me take you back to the year 1938. The world was blissfully unaware of the culinary marvel that was about to be born out of what can only be described as a failed kitchen experiment. A talented young chef named Ruth Wakefield was whipping up a batch of chocolate cookies in her Toll House Inn in Massachusetts. Ruth ran into a bit of a snack. She ran out of baker's chocolate, and so she improvised, right? She took little chunks of semi -sweet chocolate, mixed it into the dough, and expected it to melt through. Well, Ruth was shocked when she realized that the chocolate chips didn't just melt through, they stayed put, giving birth to what is now an iconic treat, which is the chocolate chip cookie. Right? Amazing. It's just fantastic what can happen when we frame failure with the proper perspective, right? Maybe for the more practical folks in the audience, let's talk about the Post -it note. The year was 1968, and a talented young scientist named Spencer Silver at 3M was setting out to build a really ultra -strong adhesive. Well, Spencer didn't do all that well and came out with a particularly weak one. He thought it was a failure, right? At first glance, this thing wasn't going to work, but it was actually his colleague, Art Fry, who had a different idea. It was Art's aha moment while singing in church choir, mind you, where he realized that maybe we could use this weak adhesive in a really interesting way. So they decided to create the sticky note, right? The Post -it note, and use it as a reusable bookmark. Its ability to stick to the surface, be removed without leaving any residue. It was an innovation that's fundamentally changed the way we take notes, track our lives, and of course, for the business owners in the room, document strategic innovation meetings every single year. Right? Incredible. And if you're not convinced, let's go to one more industry. Let's talk about healthcare. The year is 1928. We're all the way back in, you know, the roaring 20s, and ultimately, there are infectious diseases roaming the world with very, very few cures in sight. There was a Scottish bacteriologist named Alexander Fleming. He was laboring tirelessly to find a solution, and weary and likely overworked, he left a petri dish of bacteria uncovered for the night. He came back expecting this to be an abject failure. The experiment he was working on wasn't going to work, but what he found was fascinating. Unknowingly, the, excuse me, the unknowingly, there was a mold called penicillium that had infiltrated the bacteria and killed the surrounding bacteria, opening the door to the world's first antibiotic, penicillin. Crazy, right? This chance encounter with mold, born out of what some might have considered a total failure, marked the beginning of a medical revolution, saving countless lives, and shaping the future of healthcare as we know it. So, as the amazing video told you, my name is Mark Phillips. I'm the founder and managing partner of 11 Tribes Ventures. We are an early stage venture fund based out of Chicago that was actually born out of my own personal failure. We'll get into that story in a little bit, but I started a healthcare company called Diasense while going through business school. And as I'll get into, we had to shut the business down. I was recently asked, what's the single most important experience of your life outside of faith and family, right? Those two things kind of take the cake. But what happened in your professional life that's really shaped the way that you perceive the world? For me, the answer to that question at first glance was, well, I started a company. I learned so much about managing a business and managing people and bringing my faith into intersection with my work. But as I reflected on the question, what I realized was shutting a company down was so much more impactful to my life. It taught me so much more about myself, taught me so much more about my relationship with God. And what I'm here to talk to you today about is really that idea of failure. I think this word failure gets a bad rap in our society, right? But ultimately, we have some questions that we can ask, right? Is failure fatal? What can we learn from it? What does God have to tell us about what failure does for our personal and professional and faith lives? And ultimately, I hope to show you that in order to understand God's full vision for our personal and professional lives, we must first experience a sense of emotional and spiritual poverty. We must experience failure. And I've used this phrase, really take a downward journey. So to frame the conversation, I want to start with the story from the Bible. Great place to start, right? And it's a story that maybe you haven't heard applied to the world of business before. It's the story of Joseph. We all know the basic tenets, right? Joseph is the most favored son. His brothers stage his death and sell him into slavery. He's manipulated and imprisoned while a slave in Potiphar's home. And ultimately, while in prison, he interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and his baker. But there's some aspects of this story that I think are a little bit more underappreciated, shall we say. Let's start with the first that I think Joseph may have been a fairly intolerable little brother. Let's think about this, right? He walks around with fancy new clothes that his dad gave him. He tells his brothers that he's going to rule over them one day. If anyone has siblings, I'm the littlest brother of four brothers. If anyone has siblings, you know that is not a recipe for success. This shows me that Joseph hadn't been humbled yet. He had a vision. Yes, God gave him a vision. This is the really critical point here. He had a vision that God had given him to rule over his brothers. But that vision was so entirely far away from what God actually had in store. So yes, we're given visions, but we have to take this downward journey to fully understand and appreciate what God has in store for us. Second point, he remained obedient. Critical. Critical. Critical. God doesn't call us to success. He calls us to obedience. And let's look at the points where Joseph remained obedient. Well, he remained obedient against temptation while in Potiphar's home. He remained obedient in the depths of the prison when he probably thought his life was over. He could have said, I've got these skills God has given me. I can interpret dreams. But what's the point? What's the point? I'm just going to give up. And so that brings me to the third point, which is definitely the most important. Joseph gave God the glory. Joseph gave God the glory. Let's look at a verse from Genesis 41 to kind of unpack this. So Pharaoh, this, okay, so he's interpreted the dreams for cupbearer and baker. Pharaoh heard about it and he's calling Joseph up out of prison. Genesis 41, 14 says, So Pharaoh sent for Joseph and he was quickly brought from the dungeon. When he had shaved and changed his clothes, he came before Pharaoh. Pharaoh said to him, I had a dream and no one can interpret it. But I've heard it said of you that when you hear a dream, you can interpret it. Here's the most important verse. I cannot do it, Joseph replied to Pharaoh. But God will give Pharaoh the answer he desires. What a crazy verse. Let's put this into context, right? Think of the most powerful person in the world and then multiply that times 100. That's Pharaoh. One word out of his mouth and everything changes in Joseph's life. Joseph, I can promise you that if the president of United States comes up to me and says, Mark, you've got a special skill. Can you do it? The first words out of my mouth would be like, no, I'm sorry. I can't. So sorry. It would be, sure, let me deliver. But Joseph was humbled. He had taken the downward journey. And what he had realized was it wasn't about him. It was about God. And so I'd like to reframe verse 16 and use it as a framework for the rest of our conversation. Joseph's response is, can you interpret James? He says, no, I can't. But I serve the one who can. That's what he's saying here. And I think that's what a true humbling experience will do for us. So from here, I want to take you for three stories. Three stories from the marketplace that have occurred over the last handful of years that I think will hopefully illuminate the idea of what does this downward journey look like? And how does it ultimately bring to light God's true vision for our personal and professional careers? The first story is actually incredibly personal to me because it's about my dad. My father's name is Rich Phillips. He served for 35 years as a corporate attorney working for a small little company called Accenture, if anybody knows it. He was with them in the late 90s when they were Anderson Consulting and so helped navigate them through the Arthur Anderson and the Enron scandal, which is a whole story in and of itself. But ultimately, my dad spent his whole majority of his career with Accenture. He was given an opportunity, actually, towards the later half of his career to pursue the general counsel position of the company. And if you know anything about big corporate structures and general counsel positions, what my dad understood was that role, it really would put into conflict for him his priorities. What do I mean by that? I mean, his priorities were, number one, to be a present husband and father. Well, let me flip that. Number one, to be a child of God. Number two, to be a present husband and father. I was still a sophomore in high school when my dad was offered the opportunity. so here's the punchline. He turned it down. He turned down the general counsel position of Accenture. But here's the thing. God honored it. And to me, that rejection, that decision my dad made to take the path less traveled, if you will, that was his downward journey. Well, about three years after that decision was made, my dad was approached by the CEO of Accenture, a gentleman named Pierre Nanturn. And Pierre said, Rich, I need you to rewrite the conduct policy for Accenture. We haven't rewritten it in about 30 years. It needs an overhaul. Would you do it? My dad graciously and humbly accepted the role. And wouldn't you know it, the next Sunday at church, we're sitting there, I'm sitting right next to him, and the sermon series that was being started that week was a book on Proverbs and the everlasting and enduring nature of the wisdom of Proverbs. My dad had the inspiration that he needed. He spent six months pouring over the book of Proverbs, pulling out the salient wisdom that he felt like was good for not just our personal lives, but our professional and our business lives as well. Things like, kind words bring life, but cruel words crush, Proverbs 15.4. Or lazy hands make for poverty, and diligent hands bring wealth. My dad created a new conduct policy within Accenture, and he presented the new policy along with a specific action plan that tied global managing partner compensation to the adherence of the conduct policy. So let's put this into context, what's happening right now. These super powerful Accenture executives are being tied to biblical wisdom in the form of Proverbs. My dad didn't call it biblical. He didn't call it Christian. He called it conduct counts. He said, these are enduring truths that we know to be good, and this is how we should operate our business. He presented it to the board of directors of Accenture, and wouldn't you know it, it was unanimously ratified. I took a screenshot. I wish you could see it a little bit more closely, but on your phones, if you want to go to Accenture Code of Business Ethics, you'll pull up, make your conduct count. This was my father's work, and I'm incredibly proud of him, and I think he would tell you if he was up here, this was the most important thing he did from a professional perspective. But let me tie it back to our conversation today. Traditional advice would have been to take the opportunity to gain influence, become general counsel, and pursue a bigger role, but my dad chose a different path. He chose to be obedient to what he knew were his key priorities, and ultimately God honored that in an incredible way. The second story is that of an organization called Kehi Food Distributors. It's a local firm, actually, in Chicago. It's one of the largest food distributors in the world. I had the pleasure of meeting a gentleman named Rusty Bland, who's a 20 -year executive there, and now the executive director of the Kehi Cares Foundation. Rusty started at the firm in the early 2000s, and he had a vision while he was there for, man, what would it look like if we built a kingdom -based culture within our company that when people came to work, no matter their faith affiliations, they would leave with more in the tank than when they had arrived? I think this is a beautiful question, and one that we as believers can bring to the marketplace in so many different ways. Well, Rusty struggled with this for years. Year over year, would come up with new ideas how to build this culture, how to bring it to life, until in 2010, he took a trip with a few select colleagues to Honduras. They were headed there to help build the trees for impoverished communities, but as Rusty leaned into that experience, he found a vision for this kingdom -based culture. He was going to Honduras to heal, but ultimately he was the one being healed. And as he was going to serve, he was the one being served. In our culture, our Western American thinking is success is always framed as up and to the right, but upwardly mobile is a sentiment. But let's go back to the teachings of Jesus, right? What has Jesus taught us? He said things like, if you want to find your life, you must lose it first. He taught about how seeds don't really become what they're fully intended to be until they fall to the ground and die, and then they can multiply. That is the downward journey, isn't it? As business leaders, we must do the same. And while it is counterintuitive to culture, when we empty ourselves too, and we take this downward journey, we find our lives and experience the fullest life and the fullest business possible. Today, Rusty learned that in Honduras and brought this simple insight back to his company. All 400 senior executive level folks at Kehi take a trip to Honduras or elsewhere to perform some sort of mission trip every single year. That's regardless of their faith affiliations. That has ultimately led to a business culture that is built upon servant leadership and creates real value for each and every one of their employees. I don't think it's any accident that Kehi has since become the second largest food distributor in the world and recently surpassed a billion dollars in revenue. It's amazing. One more story for you from the marketplace, and then we'll watch a brief video. I'm honored to know a man named Pete Oaks. I wonder, I actually buy a show of hands. Does anyone else here know Pete Oaks? Can we get, yeah, I see a few hands out there. Incredible man, lives in Kansas. If you ever get the chance to meet him, I highly encourage it. He's one of the most God -honoring business leaders I've ever met. I called him in anticipation of this conversation with all of you, and I said, Pete, what was that downward journey like for you? When did you know that you had to humble yourself to become successful? And for those of you that know him, Pete didn't skip a beat, and in his low, powerful voice, Pete said, Mark, I was 41 years old. I was in the middle of a bad business deal, and I was about to go completely broke. I'd bought a bank, a failing bank at that, and we were being sued. And in my great wisdom, I decided to countersue, and I was burning $8,000 a day in legal fees. It's crazy. Desperate for resolution, desperate for a way out, Pete felt the Lord telling him to humble himself, empty his pride, to take the downward journey. Humbled and broken, Pete walked into the office of the man that was suing him. He dropped to his knees. This is a big man. Dropped to his knees and said, begged for forgiveness, begged for resolution. And here's the craziest part. As he looked up, he saw that the man had begun to weep. He was so overcome with emotion. He looked down at Pete and said, just one month prior, that he'd accepted Jesus Christ into his heart as his Lord and Savior. He was so frustrated with the mess that this lawsuit had created, that all he'd been asking God for was a way out. A way to end the debate. To end the lawsuit. The two men sat down. They agreed on terms. And to the chagrin of their legal teams, of course, they ended the lawsuit. At the age of 41, for the first time in his life, Pete realized that, as he says it, God's word makes good sense. God will get you to this emptied out place. But it's either going to be voluntarily or involuntarily. It's up to us to choose how. Pete has since gone on to form a company called Capital Three, which is focused on impact investing. And I'd like to play a brief video that really, it brings something to light, which I'll touch on after the video. But when we take this downward journey, what it allows us to do is to take the pressure off of ourselves and to co -create with our creator. I think Pete has done that in an exceptional and a beautiful way. And as he's building a business in a maximum security prison, which you'll hear about in just 10 seconds, I think Pete has brought incredible impact to the marketplace in a way that very few have. And I'm here today to tell you that is a problem and that will lead to so much pain. I look back on it now and again, I was asked, what's the single most important experience of your life? That failure behind meeting Jesus Christ and meeting my wife, that failure is the single most important experience of my life. And I think it is the single greatest gift God has ever given me. It showed me that my identity is not in my company. It showed me that my self -worth is tied to my relationship with Jesus and not the thing that I can build. And so I shut diacence down. I became very passionate about the topic of failure, obviously, but I wanted to do something about it. And to use the Joseph story, I felt God give me a vision to think about how do we support entrepreneurs? I think in the world of business and for my purposes, startups, we've got two connected but not correlated outcomes. The business outcome is what, as a society, we are trained to measure. Exit valuations and cash flow and IRR, all the things, right? But the other side of the equation is just as important. But we don't talk about it as often. We've coined it the founder outcome, the CEO outcome, whatever phrase you want to use. As a startup investor, we focus on founders. And what I believe is that traditional venture capital and traditional capitalism is focused on a maximization function. It wants to maximize for financial outcomes. But true capitalism, and as you heard Pete say, it's not just about the financial, it's an optimization function. How do we optimize for business? Excuse me. How do we optimize for financial, for human, for social, and for environmental capital? That's what we're focused on. so at 11 Tribes, we exist not just to build for business outcomes, but we invest to optimize for both founder and business outcomes. How do we do that? Well, a couple of different ways. We allocate 2 % of every invested dollar directly to the entrepreneurs we work with for them to put towards their own entrepreneurial resilience. We talked about ILI, training and equipping leaders to have an impact in the marketplace. We can't expect them to go out and be successful right off the bat. They need training. They need to be equipped. So that work of ILI and so many other leadership development agencies across the country is just incredible. We also bring around the entrepreneurs we work with, subject matter experts who also understand that, man, life isn't just about having successful financial outcomes. It's about building in a way that's sustainable and in a way that makes life worth living to keep it very simple. And so that's what we're doing at 11 Tribes Ventures. I am so passionate about failure and the idea that we don't have to have all the answers. How do we co -create with our creator? These are the things that I really want us to be thinking about. And so as I close my remarks, there's a few questions that I would ask, right? If we can't trust God in our own disappointment, how can we expect to trust him with fulfilled dreams? Ephesians 3.20 says, God is able to do exceedingly, abundantly, and above all you could ever ask, imagine, or think, according to his power at work in you, to him be the glory. What a powerful verse. Have you ever wondered if greatness can be born from endless failure? Imagine a silent room filled only with shadows. Every shadow hides a moment of defeat. Yet beyond those shadows, a faint light promises hope. Long ago, in a small American town, a young man named Abraham Lincoln dreamed of making a difference. He looked out at the sunrise every morning, filled with hope. At 21, Abraham started his first business, eager to find success. Soon it failed, leaving him with nothing but empty pockets and a heavy heart. Despite his first loss, Abraham tried again, running for local legislature. He lost the election, listening as others celebrated their own victories. Unwilling to give up, Abraham started another business at 24. This venture failed as well, leaving him deeper in debt. At 26, Abraham's beloved passed away. Alone beneath a tree, he grieved in silence, his spirit nearly broken. Sadness and loss grew until one year later, Abraham suffered a nervous breakdown. Abraham at home, resting by a simple fireplace, trying to heal. With slow steps, Abraham found strength to try again. At 34, he ran for Congress, but voters turned him away once more. Year after year, Abraham faced new defeats. At 45, he lost the Senate race and walked home under a silent sky. Even after all the losses, Abraham kept trying. At 47, he hoped to become vice president. Again, he failed. At 49, he tried for the Senate once more. Another loss. Each setback pushed him to reflect and grow. Finally, after decades of struggle, at 52, Abraham won the presidency. His voice rang with hope as crowds cheered. Across the ocean, in 1913, Lee DeForest, a clever inventor, tried to make voices travel across the sea, but no one believed him. When Lee shared his idea, many experts laughed and called him a liar. At a public meeting, reporters shouted and accused him. Even after such embarrassment, Lee pressed on, alone at night. He worked hard on his invention, sparks flying as he adjusted wires. In the end, Lee's invention changed everything. With his tube, the world could hear voices across the ocean at last. A few years earlier, in their simple bicycle shop, two brothers, Orville and Wilbur Wright, dreamed of flying like birds. People mocked the Wright brothers, calling their project foolish. A newspaper said heavier than air flight was impossible. The brothers did not listen to doubts. At Kitty Hawk, they built a strange, fragile -looking flying machine. On a windy morning, Orville piloted the first flight. The odd machine rose, carrying hope with it into the air. A few decades later, in Kentucky, an elderly man named Colonel Harlan Sanders stared sadly at his last few bills, searching for a way to survive. With only his car and his mother's recipe, Colonel Sanders filled boxes with fried chicken and set off down the road, praying for a miracle. Day after day, Sanders knocked on doors. He heard no more than a thousand times. Still, he did not quit. At last, someone gave him a chance. Colonel Sanders' recipe brought smiles, and soon, many people lined up for his chicken. Across the country, a young man named Walt Disney showed his drawings to newspapers. But editors dismissed him, saying he had no talent. Rejected and broke, Walt worked alone in a tiny shed overrun by mice. Still, he sketched, dreaming of brighter days. Watching the busy mice, Walt got an idea. With renewed energy, he drew a cheerful mouse and called him Mickey. Mickey Mouse soon danced across movie screens, sparking worldwide smiles. Walt's failures became stepping stones to his greatest triumph. Elsewhere, a teacher called a young Thomas Edison, too stupid to learn. He left school with barely three months of lessons. With his mother's love, Thomas learned at home. He studied by candlelight, asking questions and taking notes. Years later, partly deaf, Thomas used his curiosity to invent. He built strange gadgets, always experimenting and learning. Through countless failures, Thomas' hard work brought the world bright lights and music machines. Not far away,

[None]
a

[SPEAKER_00]
clever man named Henry Ford built his first car, forgetting an important detail, the reverse gear. Instead of quitting, Henry fixed his mistake and tried again, changing how people travel forever. Would you call these people failures? They did not give up when times were tough. Their greatest gift was their will to rise again. One day, disaster struck Thomas Edison again. At 67, he watched in horror as his factory burned to the ground. Yet Thomas did not mourn for long. He told his friends, All our mistakes are burnt up. We can start again. Only three weeks later, Edison unveiled his next invention, the phonograph, turning disaster into another triumph. Every person in these stories chose not to stop at failure. Because of that, our world is brighter, safer and more fun. Greatness isn't about never falling down. It's about refusing to stay down and standing up always one more time. Real greatness is not about never failing, but about always rising after you fall. As Tom Watson Sr. said, If you want to succeed, double your failure rate. And so all of these areas of work and the intentionality that needs to be brought there, if there's one thought from today, really it is that planning aspect and getting out in front of it.

Welcome dear viewers to an exploration into a world often overlooked. Today we're diving into the fascinating world of mosses and uncovering why they are the unsung heroes of our ecosystems. From the lush rainforests to the arid deserts, mosses can be found in every corner of our planet. These ancient plants some dating back millions of years, hold secrets vital to the health and balance of our natural world. Join me as we delve into the intricate lives of mosses, revealing their remarkable adaptations and crucial roles in supporting biodiversity. Though diminutive in size, mosses play a monumental role in shaping the landscapes they inhabit. Picture a barren rocky terrain. It is here that mosses first take hold, their tenacious rhizoids anchoring them to the unforgiving surface. These delicate root -like structures not only provide stability but also begin the slow, patient process of breaking down rock, contributing to the formation of soil. As mosses spread, they act as nature's weavers, binding the soil together, preventing erosion, and creating a sanctuary for other plants to take root. Mosses create intricate micro -habitats within their verdant layers. Insects find refuge in their damp embrace, sheltering from predators and the harsh elements. Amphibians, too, benefit from the mosses' moisture -retaining properties, providing a safe haven for egg -laying and the development of their young. Mosses are the epitome of resilience, possessing an almost mythical ability to withstand nature's extremes. When faced with drought, mosses enter a dormant state, surviving for months, even years, with virtually no water. Once rain returns, they miraculously revive, their emerald hues returning with a vibrancy that speaks of life renewed. Freezing temperatures pose little threat to these hardy survivors. Their cells possess a unique ability to withstand the formation of ice crystals, which would be fatal to most plants. In environments prone to wildfires, mosses play a crucial role in post -fire recovery. Their resilience in the face of environmental challenges makes them pioneers, paving the way for the regeneration and flourishing of entire ecosystems. Venture into any moss -carpeted forest and you'll discover a world teeming with life. Insects, the foundation of many food chains, find both sustenance and shelter within the moss's embrace. Springtails navigate the intricate network of moss stems while tiny mites graze on the microscopic organisms that thrive in this damp environment. Birds weave mosses into their nests, providing a safe and comfortable haven for their young. Small mammals seek refuge among the mosses, creating burrows and tunnels that wind through their dense growth. Some species of insects have evolved specialized adaptations to mimic the appearance of mosses, camouflaging themselves against predators or unsuspecting prey. This intricate web of life, woven together by the presence of mosses, highlights their importance in maintaining biodiversity. Their ability to create microhabitats and support a wide range of species makes them crucial components of healthy and balanced ecosystems. For centuries, mosses have held a place of honor in traditional medicine. Modern science is beginning to unlock the secrets behind these ancient remedies, revealing a treasure trove of bioactive compounds with exciting potential for pharmaceuticals and cosmetics. Deep within the cellular structure of mosses lie a diverse array of chemical compounds, many of which are unique to these ancient plants. One promising area of research is in the field of antibiotic resistance. Preliminary studies have shown that extracts from certain moss species exhibit antibacterial activity against a range of harmful bacteria. Their extracts have also shown promise in skin care and wound healing. Some moss species possess potent antioxidant properties which can help protect skin from damage caused by free radicals. As research into the medicinal properties of mosses continues, we are likely to uncover even more ways in which these ancient plants can contribute to human health and well -being. As our planet grapples with the escalating consequences of climate change, mosses emerge as unlikely heroes. Unlike trees which store carbon primarily in their woody biomass, mosses excel at capturing carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere and locking it away in the soil. In peat bogs, vast wetlands dominated by sphagnum mosses, this carbon sequestration process is particularly pronounced. These peatlands, often referred to as carbon sinks, play a crucial role in regulating Earth's climate. They are estimated to store twice as much carbon as all the world's forests combined, making their preservation paramount in the fight against climate change. Beyond peat bogs, mosses and other ecosystems also contribute significantly to carbon sequestration. Understanding and harnessing the carbon -capturing power of mosses becomes increasingly vital. Antarctica, a continent of stark beauty and unforgiving conditions, seems an unlikely place for life to thrive. Yet, even in this frozen desert, life finds a way. Among the hardiest of survivors are the mosses, tenacious pioneers clinging to life in this most extreme of environments. Antarctic mosses have evolved remarkable adaptations to endure the relentless challenges of their frozen world. During the long, dark winter months, Antarctic mosses enter a state of dormancy, their metabolic processes slowing to a crawl. When the sun finally reappears, Antarctic mosses spring back to life with astonishing speed. Their photosynthetic machinery captures every precious photon of sunlight to fuel their growth and reproduction. Their presence, a testament to the tenacity of life, paints the icy landscapes with splashes of vibrant green. Imagine a landscape painted in hues of emerald and gold, a mosaic of waterlogged bogs and spongy hummocks stretching as far as the eye can see. This is the realm of the peatlands, ancient ecosystems shaped by the tireless work of mosses, particularly the remarkable sphagnum moss. These seemingly desolate landscapes are in fact vital carbon sinks, playing a crucial role in regulating Earth's climate. Peatlands, often referred to as bogs, mires or muskegs, are formed over thousands of years through the slow accumulation of partially decayed plant matter. As sphagnum moss grows and dies, it forms layers upon layers of peat, effectively locking away the carbon it absorbed during its lifetime. Peatlands, though covering less than 3 % of Earth's land surface, store an estimated one -third of all soil carbon. Protecting peatlands from degradation and promoting their restoration is essential for mitigating climate change. Beneath the surface of rivers, lakes and streams, a hidden world teems with life. Mosses play a crucial role as ecosystem engineers, shaping the aquatic environment and influencing water quality. Their secret lies in their ability to form biofilms, complex communities of microorganisms that coat submerged surfaces. These biofilms, often invisible to the naked eye, are teeming with bacteria, algae, fungi and other microorganisms. The microorganisms within the biofilms absorb excess nutrients, pollutants and sediments from the water column, effectively purifying the water. These biofilms also provide a vital food source for a wide range of invertebrates, which in turn support larger animals higher up the food chain. Understanding the role of mosses and biofilms in aquatic ecosystems is crucial for managing water quality and conserving these precious resources. For centuries, mosses have been relegated to the sidelines of the design world. But in recent years, these humble plants have experienced a resurgence of interest, their unique qualities embraced by architects and designers seeking sustainable and biophilic solutions. One of the most promising applications of mosses in modern architecture is in the creation of green roofs. Mosses with their shallow root systems, low water requirements and ability to thrive in harsh conditions, make ideal candidates for green roof installations. Mosses are also finding their way into vertical gardens, living walls that bring a touch of nature to urban environments. Interior designers are incorporating mosses into their creations, using them to create living walls, moss art installations, and even moss furniture. Beyond aesthetics and sustainability, mosses offer practical benefits in landscape architecture, stabilizing soil, and preventing erosion. For millennia, mosses have held a place of honor in traditional medicine systems around the world. In Chinese medicine, mosses have been used for centuries to treat a range of ailments, including burns, wounds, and skin infections. Native American tribes have also incorporated mosses into their traditional medicine practices for generations. Sphagnum moss in particular was highly valued for its absorbent and antiseptic properties. While modern medicine has often overlooked traditional remedies, recent scientific research has begun to validate the efficacy of some of these ancient practices. Studies have shown that certain moss species possess antibacterial, antiviral, and anti -inflammatory properties. By bridging the gap between ancient wisdom and modern science, we can unlock the full potential of these remarkable plants to improve human health and well -being. From the lush carpets of ancient forests to the frozen expanse of Antarctica, mosses have proven themselves to be the unsung heroes of the plant world. Their role in shaping ecosystems, supporting biodiversity, combating climate change, and offering potential solutions for medicine and sustainable design is nothing short of remarkable. These miniature marvels, often overlooked, deserve our admiration and protection. Thank you for joining me on this exploration. Like, comment, and subscribe to join me on future adventures into the wonders of our natural world.

Welcome back to Stoics Decoded, where we dive into timeless wisdom and try to decode its meaning for our lives today. I'm not an expert here. I'm a fellow traveler on this journey of growth and understanding, applying these lessons as we go. And today, allow me to introduce to you the giants of Stoicism, Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, and Seneca. Let's meet the minds behind the philosophy. First, we have Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor often called the Philosopher King. Imagine leading an entire empire while also contemplating the meaning of life. His personal journal Meditations wasn't meant to be published. It was his private guide to staying calm, rational, and virtuous amid the chaos of ruling. This idea of focusing on what's within our control resonates deeply. How often do we waste energy worrying about things we can't change? Marcus reminds us to ground ourselves in what we can control—our thoughts, actions, and attitudes. And believe me, I still am learning how to apply this myself. Next, we meet Epictetus, a man who started life as a slave and rose to become one of Stoicism's most influential teachers. His story is a testament to resilience. Epictetus taught that true freedom comes not from external circumstances, but from mastering our inner world. This teaching hits home, doesn't it? We can't control life's curveballs, but we can control how we respond to them. That's something we're constantly working on—catching ourselves in those moments when frustration or fear kicks in, and asking, how can I respond better? Finally, there's Seneca, a man of contrasts. He was a wealthy statesman and advisor to Emperor Nero, but his writings reflect deep insights into living simply and meaningfully. In his essays and letters, Seneca emphasizes that life is short and urges us to live with purpose. This one stings, doesn't it? It's a wake -up call for how much time we spend on distractions instead of what truly matters. Seneca's advice is like a mirror, challenging us to rethink our priorities. So what do these three have in common? They teach us to master ourselves, face adversity with courage, and focus on what truly matters. Their wisdom is practical, timeless, and honestly, not always easy to follow. But that's okay. We're here to grow, not to be perfect. Here are three takeaways we're trying to live by, and we invite you to try them too. 1. From Marcus Aurelius, focus on what's within your control. Let go of the rest. 2. From Epictetus, your reaction defines your experience. Pause and choose your response. 3. From Seneca, reflect daily on how you're spending your time. Are you wasting it or investing it? These are just glimpses into the lives and teachings of the great Stoics. There's so much more to learn, and I'm excited to keep exploring with you. In the labyrinth of existence, where the shadows of adversity loom large, the Stoic figures of ancient wisdom stand as eternal beacons, guiding us through the tumultuous seas of life. Their tales, etched in the annals of time, narrate not only the struggles, but also the triumphs of those who embrace Stoicism with a fervor that transcends the ages. As we traverse these narratives, we find ourselves intertwined with the Stoic ethos, a collective journey towards self -control, fortitude, and the conquest of destructive emotions. In the realm of Stoicism, we discover not just philosophers, but warriors of the mind who face challenges with unwavering resolve. Consider the words of Seneca, the Stoic sage, who once remarked, For it is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste much of it. In this simple yet profound statement lies the essence of Stoic philosophy, an invitation to seize each moment, to cultivate mindfulness, and to confront the transient nature of our existence. Epictetus, the slave -turned -philosopher, echoes this sentiment with his teachings on the dichotomy of control. We cannot choose our external circumstances, but we can always choose how we respond to them. In these words, we find the cornerstone of Stoicism, a call to direct our focus inward, to master our reactions, and to find strength in the face of adversity. Drawing inspiration from the imperial Stoic, Marcus Aurelius, we confront the harsh realities of life with a resolute mind. It is not death that a man should fear, but he should fear never beginning to live. Aurelius, the philosopher king, beckons us to embrace life fully, to recognize that true living lies in the pursuit of virtue and wisdom. The Stoic path is not devoid of challenges, rather, it is a journey illuminated by the sagas of those who embraced life's tribulations with grace. As we tread this path, we sense a collective resonance, aurelius feeling, connecting us to the timeless wisdom of Stoicism. In the crucible of existence, where shadows yield to the indomitable light of the Stoic spirit, we find solace. Let these tales resonate within, awakening a profound desire for self -mastery, fortitude, and the unwavering pursuit of a life well lived. For in the annals of Stoicism, we discover not just stories, but timeless echoes that beckon us to rise above, to conquer, and to embody the essence of true resilience. pence.

Don't mess with ale if you are weak. A clear head is good company. Drinking is a dangerous friend. Too much ale and a man's heart is laid open for all to see. All the people need in order to rise up against tyranny is a leader bold enough to take up the banner. The more folks stand in the way of two hearts that yearn for each other, the hotter the flame of love waxes. Only a coward waits to be taken like a lamb from the fold or a fox from a trap. When fear leads the way, the destination is never glorious. The error is the result of letting fear rule your actions. To become a man that instantly commands respect. Don't be afraid to be criticized or disliked. Don't be afraid to engage in conflict and stand up for what is right. Even a silent man will be instantly respected if he tells the truth. As one candle can light another, so too can greatness of mind be transferred amongst men. To remain in solitude is to deprive oneself of this kindling. Even in the sheath, the sword must be sharp. So too must the mind and the spirit be within the body. Life is not a level field. Life is hills and mountains, lowlands and ravines. There is more honor in accumulating little by little than in reaching for the sky and ending up flat on your face. You will reach your destination even though you travel slowly. When truth and fairness are different from what is law, better it is to follow truth and fairness. Honest conflict is always better than dishonest harmony. Better to die with honor than live with shame. Where wolf's ears are, wolf's teeth are near. The foolish man thinks he will live forever if he keeps away from fighting. But old age won't grant him a truce even if the spears do. Oftentimes it is not numbers that wins the victory, but those who fare forward with the most vigor. When men meet foes in fight, a stout heart is better than a sharp sword. The brave man shall fight and win, though dull his blade may be. When a real battle starts, you'll always find that there is no bravest man. Stand by your own trial and not by what others say. A person should not agree today to what he will regret tomorrow. Real warriors don't show their hearts until an axe cuts open their chests. That which has a bad beginning is likely to have a bad ending. Not every cloud which darkens the day brings rain. Take care of your speech. It can be the catalyst for many needless problems. You never know who could be lending an ear to your ramblings. No one is the total fool if he knows when to hold his tongue. Gold shines bright, but honor outlasts even the sun. The storm makes the oak take deeper root. Hardship forges the strongest souls. A ship does not sail on yesterday's wind, move forward or be left behind. Fate may weave the thread, but his warrior chooses how to face it. Here are some key takeaways from cats on how to be resilient. Embrace independence. Cats show us the value of self -reliance and the ability to bounce back on our own when faced with challenges. For example, a person who lives alone and learns to be self -sufficient can better handle unexpected situations like a power outage or a sudden illness. They are less likely to panic and more able to adapt and problem -solve on their own. However, it's important to note that being self -reliant doesn't mean isolating oneself from others. In fact, strong social connections and support systems are crucial for resilience. A person who relies solely on themselves may struggle to cope with more complex challenges that require the help and expertise of others. Be adaptable. Cats are known for their ability to adapt to different environments and situations. Being flexible and open to change can help us be more resilient in the face of adversity. For example, a person who loses their job may need to adapt by learning new skills or exploring different career paths. They may reach out to their social network for support and guidance or seek professional help from a career counselor. By being adaptable and willing to seek help, this person can overcome the setback and emerge stronger and more resilient. However, there are situations where being too adaptable can be detrimental. For instance, constantly changing one's values or beliefs to fit in with different social circles may lead to a lack of authenticity and a loss of one's true identity. Stay curious. Cats are naturally curious creatures, always exploring and learning new things. Adopting a similar mindset can help us stay engaged and motivated, even when things get tough. Take time to rest. Cats are experts at self -care, knowing when to rest and recharge. Prioritizing our own well -being is crucial for building resilience in the long term. Stay alert. Cats are always aware of their surroundings, ready to pounce at a moment's notice. Staying alert and aware can help us anticipate challenges and respond quickly when they arise. Be patient. Cats are known for their patience, waiting for the right moment to strike. Learning to be patient in the face of adversity can help us stay focused on our goals and persevere through difficult times. Find joy in small things. Cats find joy in simple pleasures like playing with a toy or basking in the sun. Cultivating gratitude for small moments of happiness can help us maintain a positive outlook even during tough times. Stay curious. Cats are naturally curious creatures, always exploring and learning new things. Staying curious can help us stay engaged and motivated, even when things get tough. Stay active. Cats are always on the move, whether they're playing or hunting. Staying active can help us maintain our physical and mental health, which is essential for resilience. Take time to rest. Cats also know the importance of rest and relaxation. Taking breaks and giving ourselves time to recharge can help us stay resilient in the long run. Be resourceful. Cats are masters of using what they have to get what they want. Being resourceful can help us find creative solutions to problems and overcome obstacles. Practice mindfulness. Cats are experts at living in the moment and being present. Practicing mindfulness can help us stay focused on the present. Adaptability. Cats are masters of adapting to different environments and situations. Being flexible and open to change helps us navigate unexpected circumstances. Confidence. Cats display self -assurance and believe in their abilities. Building self -confidence enables us to face difficulties with resilience and determination. Focus on self -care. Cats prioritize their well -being by resting, grooming, and nourishing themselves. Taking care of our physical and mental health enhances our resilience. Persistence. Cats exemplify persistence in pursuing their goals. They remind us to persevere despite setbacks and keep striving for what we want. Agility. Cats agility allows them to quickly navigate obstacles. Being mentally and emotionally agile helps us adapt and find solutions in challenging situations. Curiosity and continuous learning. Cats are naturally curious and constantly explore their surroundings. Cultivating curiosity and a love for learning helps us adapt and grow. Embracing solitude. Cats value their alone time. Taking moments of solitude can help us reflect, rejuvenate, and build resilience. By incorporating these qualities into our lives, we can learn from the resilience of cats and cultivate our own strength in the face of adversity.

This is the Investor Connect podcast program. I'm Hal T. Martin. I'm the host of the show in which we interview angel investors, venture capital, family offices, private equity, and many other investors for early stage and growth companies. I hope you enjoy this episode. Investor Connect is a 501c3 nonprofit dedicated to the education of investors and startups for fundraising. Please consider donating $100 to the program to help others in their investor and entrepreneur journey. You can find the donate button on the InvestorConnect.org website. Well, hello. This is Hal Marchant with Investor Connect. Today, I'm here with Christina Chappell, director of 11 Tribe Ventures. 11 Tribes Ventures is an early stage venture fund that proactively invests in the well -being of entrepreneurs. The company provides innovative, founder -focused venture capital investment to early stage technology companies in non -traditional technology hubs across the country. Christina, thank you for joining us.

[SPEAKER_00]
Paul, it is so great to be here. Thank you for having me.

[SPEAKER_01]
So tell us more about your background before joining 11 Tribe Ventures.

[SPEAKER_00]
Yes. So 11 Tribes is based in Chicago, and I drove up here six months ago from the South without a friend or family member in sight because I was so compelled by the thesis of what we're building here. I have a background in city planning and entrepreneurship. Back home in Atlanta, I launched two community engagement initiatives, one at my school and one in the greater Atlanta community, which both scaled up and brought me to UNC Chapel Hill on scholarship with a program called Moorhead Cain, which punted me into a number of different environments, giving me experience in teaching and consulting. One of my summer internships, I ended up at a private equity firm, and that was my first experience into the world of finance and loved that, but wanted to move earlier stage. And so I've found 11 Tribes. I really appreciated our thesis and really how we were able to integrate our values with our work. And that's what made me decide to move to Chicago to join full -time as employee number one to the managing partner, Mark Phillips.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. So what excites you right now?

[None]
You

[SPEAKER_00]
know, something that I found very exciting, Paul, is just the rise of remote and hybrid work. We're finding entrepreneurs who are tucked away in what we call competitive geographies. So non -traditional tech hubs, so not San Francisco or New York, more like Chattanooga and Cincinnati and Indianapolis who are building great businesses. And also given just our current macroeconomic environment here in February of 2023, we're seeing tons of big tech layups. So I think that some great companies are going to be formed in these days. And I'm also just personally excited to be placed here in Chicago. There are several funds here who are working to activate more early stage capital and more LPs from the women and wealthy individuals in the area who have not had exposure to venture capital as an asset class before. So I'm excited to be investing in this time.

Yes. For LPs, I think the first, and it's top of mind, is just finding a firm that you are aligned with from a values perspective. And if you're able to find a team deploying capital in a way that you think are advancing good outside of just financial returns, I think that that is really special, especially if you are running checks into early stage funds, possibly for the first time. And I also would give advice of finding teams who will be transparent with you. I know here at 11 Tribes, we are committed to full transparency with our LPs. So the other piece of advice I would give is founders are looking for more than just financial capital these days. So as an emerging fund, we have to be really clear of what's our value add and our niche alongside of the check that we're writing and how can we get access to the best cap tables and the best co -investors.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. Well, tell us more about that. How do you see the industry evolving from here with that in mind?

And so who is getting the checks written? And then who are the LPs in these funds? I think that I'm seeing evolution there. And I mean, for Fund Two at 11 Tribes, we're doing a parallel fund structure that allows more people to participate by giving flexibility on minimums too. So we're seeing more and more creative ways for funds to establish themselves and engage more people who've maybe not had exposure to the asset class before.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. And what do think is the biggest change we're going to see in the VC fund world in the next few years?

[SPEAKER_00]
I think what we have seen is that there's more and more competition with just the number of emerging funds and smaller players raising first -time funds or second funds. And I think that raises the bar and elevates the industry as a whole. So that's something that's very exciting to me. And I also think that that is actually breeding more collaboration in the industry. I know we have gotten sharper on who do we want to invest alongside. And that's going to, what we believe, increase the pie for everyone and venture as a whole too.

[SPEAKER_01]
Great. Well, so let's talk about your investment thesis. What exactly is it and how did you arrive at it?

[SPEAKER_00]
Yeah, we do take a thesis -driven approach here at 11 Tribes. And we have three main components to that, one of which I've spoken to, which is we target competitive geographies. And so we are a Midwest -based fund. We lean into that. And we have a strong Midwest presence in our Fund One portfolio. But we also are looking for the best builders in Atlanta, Georgia, in Columbia, South Carolina, in Texas. And so that's one angle. The next is that we are a seed stage fund. So we are some of the first checks in, typically following on with a lead investor to close that round. And the other piece that really sets us apart and the reason why I came to join the firm is just the amount of support that we assemble around our founding teams. Every check that we write, we have made a commitment to invest 2 % on top of that check directly to the founding teams for them to invest in their well -being and development. And so usually that looks like we're writing $250K to $300K checks, which means those founders are getting $5,000 to $6,000 in a bank account for them to use either on an executive coach geared specifically for founders or for a therapist. I think, I know my managing partner, Mark, has sat across the table from countless founders who have said, if only you were here five years ago when I was raising my round, then maybe I would still be married or I would still have a relationship with my children. And so we think we want to help our founders build great businesses that have the potential to affect cultures and change, but not at the expense of the things that are most important in their lives. And the other piece of what we surround our founding teams with is what we call our venture partner platform. And so we have identified industry experts and really operators who have started and exited companies scattered all around the country. I mean, most of our venture partners are located in these competitive geographies. And they come on to be a mentor and coach to that founder, getting in the trench with them. And we compensate them with GP Carey here at 11 Tribes. Yeah.

me know. Two come to mind, Hal. The first is a Chicago -based company called KeyWise AI, and they are a consumer healthcare company. We say KeyWise is a bit for your brain, basically. Through a five -year NIH -funded grant, the KeyWise team built an AI platform that tracks brain function objectively and precisely. So the KeyWise system uses keystrokes on your smartphone to measure things like processing speed, attention, impulse control, and mood stability. And their patent -protected system is currently live on the App Store. I'd encourage everyone to go download it and give it a try. The team is focused on its B2B2C growth strategy in 23. They're targeting hospital systems, clinics, and outpatient entities that will use the platform to help track patient health and adherence post -hospitalization. And the other company in our portfolio that we are really excited about is a Cincinnati -based company called GetTogether. They play in the future of workspace. And GetTogether is building the fastest, easiest way to schedule meetings by embedding AI directly into any messaging platform. So think text, Slack, Teams, and even email. And fundamentally, GetTogether believes that any human connection today starts with a message, and they want to be the platform that makes connecting frictionless. They just received follow -on capital from Drive Capital, which is one of the largest funds in the Midwest. And they just closed a patent application for their cross -channel chat AI scheduling feature, making GetTogether the only centralized scheduling AI that can be used across multiple communication channels. So we're very excited for both of those teams.

Well, sound like great startups. Congratulations on those. So what do you think are the main challenges early -stage venture funds face today?

[SPEAKER_00]
You know, venture is an industry where there can be a lot of hype and a lot of noise. And so I think for funds who maybe have less access to good deal flow, it can be difficult to remain disciplined and cut through that noise. I mean, we see ChatGPT being on every news article today. And any startup that is now touching AI or generative AI, it's easy for those valuations to become inflated. Here at 11Tribes, we really do remain disciplined. Our average valuation cap in our Fund One portfolio is just under $8 million. We made the bulk of our investments in 2021 and early 2022. So that was a time when valuations were very inflated and we were able to stay anchored. So I think that that is a challenge for an early -stage fund. And then also just making sure that you have a comprehensive due diligence process. I know here we have quite a hefty process. I run point on that. And we're not just going with even what our co -investors have to say, but we have a lot of framework on how we vet companies. And not even just the financial side or industry trends, but we also administer personality assessments to our founders with the Colby Index and StrengthsFinder to ensure that our founding teams are the best people to build and are equipped well with teammates with complementary skill sets that allow them to, what we say, ride a lion and live, which is basically what our founders are doing here.

And so I think if we are able to shift our perspective and build habits to be on the lookout for other people and make small differences or build a small amount of margin into our day to more meaningfully connect with the people around us, that that will have a massive impact on communities as a whole and our own lives as individuals.

All right, let's journey into a world smaller than the eye can see, a place filled with some of the most incredible creatures on our planet. Today we're talking about an animal so tough it makes most other life forms look fragile. This creature is the tardigrade, a microscopic animal that has been fascinating scientists for centuries. It was first discovered way back in 1773 by a German pastor named Johann August Ephraim Goese. He found these tiny critters living in water and noticed they walked with a slow lumbering gait, almost like a bear. Because of this, he gave them the wonderful nickname water bears, a name that perfectly captures their charming plodding movement. These amazing animals are true global citizens, you can find tardigrades almost anywhere on earth, proving that size has nothing to do with being a successful species. They live in the highest mountains, soaring far above the clouds and in the deepest parts of the ocean, under immense pressure. They've been discovered in the scorching heat of deserts, and in the freezing ice of Antarctica. They can even be found in your own backyard, living in the thin film of water on mosses and lichens. This incredible adaptability means that no matter where you are, you're probably not too far from a tardigrade, going about its tiny, extraordinary life. When you hear the name water bear, you might picture something cuddly, but these animals are truly unique in their appearance. They are invertebrates, meaning they don't have a backbone. Their bodies are short and plump, divided into four segments plus a head. Each of these body segments has a pair of stubby, unjointed legs, so in total, they have eight legs that they use to move around their watery world. Their slow and deliberate walk earned them their scientific name, tardigrade, which means slow stepper. They truly amble through life, taking their time as they explore their microscopic environments with a steady, unhurried pace. The discovery of tardigrades opened up a whole new understanding of what life is capable of. Before Goza spotted them under his microscope, no one could have imagined that an animal this small could be so complex and resilient. These creatures challenge our very definition of what it means to be alive and to survive. They are a testament to nature's ingenuity, showing us that even the smallest lifeforms can possess the most astonishing abilities. They are not just a scientific curiosity. They are a source of wonder and inspiration, reminding us of the hidden marvels that exist all around us, often just out of sight waiting to be discovered. Let's dive deeper into the world of the water bear and explore what makes it tick. These creatures are incredibly small, typically measuring between one -tenth to one -and -a -half millimeters long. To put that into perspective, you could line up several of them on the head of a pin. Despite their tiny size, their bodies are quite detailed. Their eight legs end in sharp claws which look like tiny hooks. These claws are made of a tough material called chitin, the same stuff that makes up the exoskeletons of insects. They use their front six legs to push themselves forward and grab onto food, while the back two legs often act as anchors, helping them hold on tight. Their anatomy is simple, but effective. Tardigrades don't have lungs or gills like many other animals do. Instead, they perform gas exchange directly through their body surface, absorbing the oxygen they need from the water around them. Their head region contains a simple brain and in many species, a pair of primitive eye cups. These eye cups don't see images like our eyes do, but they can detect light and shadow, helping the tardigrade navigate its environment. They also have sensory bristles on their bodies that can feel vibrations, allowing them to sense what's happening nearby, whether it's a potential meal or a lurking threat. When it comes to eating, tardigrades have a very specialized tool. Inside their tube -shaped mouth they have a pair of sharp needle -like structures called stylets. They use these stylets to pierce the cells of their food, which includes, media group, video of tardigrade feeding on algae, footage of tardigrade near moss under microscope at its stock, at a distribute underscore equally, algae, moss, and even other tiny invertebrates like rotifers and nematodes. Once they've pierced their target, they suck out the nutritious fluids inside, almost like they're drinking from a microscopic juice box. This method of feeding is incredibly efficient, and allows them to get the energy they need to power their tiny bodies, and survive in their often challenging habitats. There are over a thousand known species of tardigrades, and they are divided into different classes based on their features. The two main classes are the eutardigrata, and the heterotardigrata. One of the key differences between them is how their bodies are structured for reproduction and waste removal. But regardless of their specific class, all tardigrades share that same fundamental body plan, a segmented body, eight legs, and a remarkable ability to thrive in places where most other animals simply couldn't. Their simple yet powerful design is a masterclass in evolutionary efficiency, perfected over hundreds of millions of years. The life of a tardigrade is a fascinating cycle of growth and renewal. One of the most interesting things about them is a biological trait called eutile. This means that a tardigrade is born with all the cells it will ever have. As it grows from a tiny hatchling into an adult, its cells don't divide and multiply like ours do. Instead, each individual cell simply gets bigger. To accommodate this growth, a tardigrade must molt or shed its outer cuticle several times throughout its life. This process is similar to how a snake sheds its skin, allowing the animal to expand and continue its development. Reproduction for tardigrades is often tied directly to this molting process. In many species, the female lays her eggs inside her old shed cuticle. This provides a safe, protected environment for the developing embryos. After she has deposited the eggs, a male will come along and fertilize them. This courtship can be a lengthy process, sometimes lasting for over an hour, as the male ensures the next generation is secured. The eggs will then develop inside this protective casing until they are ready to hatch. At which point, tiny, fully formed tardigrades emerge, ready to begin their own journey of growth and survival. The number of eggs a female lays can vary, ranging from just a few to over a dozen, depending on the species and the environmental conditions. These eggs are just as tough as the adults, often capable of surviving many of the same extreme conditions. Once hatched, the young tardigrades look like miniature versions of the adults. They immediately begin to explore their surroundings, searching for food to fuel their growth. Each time they molt, they get a little bit bigger, until they reach their full adult size and are ready to reproduce themselves, continuing the incredible life cycle of the water bear. This cycle of molting, reproduction and growth has been repeating for an incredibly long time. Tardigrades have been on this planet for over 500 million years, which means they have survived every major mass extinction event in Earth's history, including the one that wiped out the dinosaurs. Their unique way of growing and reproducing has clearly been a successful strategy, allowing them to persist through unimaginable changes to our planet's environment. They are a living link to a deep, ancient past, and their simple yet effective life cycle is a key part of their enduring legacy as one of nature's greatest survivors. Now we get to the most famous thing about tardigrades, their unbelievable toughness. These animals can survive conditions that would be instantly fatal to almost any other form of life. One of their most incredible skills is their ability to enter a state of suspended animation called cryptobiosis. When faced with a life -threatening environment like complete dehydration, a tardigrade can expel nearly all the water from its body, up to 97 % of it. It shrivels up into a tiny, lifeless -looking ball called a ton. In this state, its metabolism slows down to almost zero, and it can wait patiently for conditions to improve. The range of extremes a tardigrade can endure is simply mind -boggling. They can survive temperatures as low as near absolute zero, which is negative 273 degrees Celsius, or negative 459 degrees Fahrenheit, and as high as 150 degrees Celsius, or 302 degrees Fahrenheit, for short periods. They can withstand pressures six times greater than those found in the deepest part of the ocean, the Mariana Trench. In 2007, scientists sent tardigrades into space on a European space agency mission. They were exposed to the vacuum of outer space and deadly solar radiation, and when they returned to Earth and were rehydrated, many of them survived and even went on to reproduce. Their ability to withstand radiation is particularly astounding. They can tolerate doses of radiation up to 1,000 times higher than the lethal dose for humans. Scientists have discovered that they have a special protein nicknamed the damage suppressor, which seems to wrap around their DNA and shield it from harm. This natural radiation shield is a subject of intense research as it could have incredible applications in medicine and technology. Furthermore, some species of tardigrades can survive without food for an astonishingly long time, potentially up to 30 years, by entering their dormant ton state and waiting for a meal to come along. It's important to clarify that tardigrades are not technically extremophiles, organisms that are adapted to live and thrive in extreme environments all the time. Instead, they are what we call extremely tolerant. They live in normal watery places but have evolved this incredible toolkit that allows them to survive temporary exposure to deadly conditions. This strategy has made them one of the most resilient animal phyla on the planet. They are a powerful reminder that, in nature, survival isn't always about being the biggest or the strongest. Sometimes it's about having the patience and the ability to endure. Lanc�or 45

In a world that seems to throw endless challenges at us, how do we maintain our composure? How do we stand strong in the face of adversity without letting external circumstances dictate our inner peace? The answer may lie in an ancient philosophy that has stood the test of time, Stoicism. Stoicism, founded in ancient Greece, teaches us that while we can't control everything that happens in life, we can control how we respond to it. In today's video, we'll dive into the key principles of Stoicism and explore how they can help us build resilience in the modern world. Welcome to the Unfolding Journey YouTube channel. Stoicism is a philosophy that originated in Athens around 300 BCE, founded by Zeno of Sidium. The Stoics believe that the ultimate goal in life is to live in harmony with nature and to develop the mental and emotional strength to navigate life's ups and downs with equanimity. It's a philosophy that champions the idea that our happiness and peace do not come from external things, but from how we choose to think and act. The Stoics recognize that life is filled with challenges, loss, hardship, disappointment, and uncertainty. But they also understood that these challenges don't have to control us. By practicing virtue, reason, and self -discipline, we can achieve a form of inner resilience that no external event can diminish. Key Principles of Stoicism. Let's take a closer look at the key Stoic principles that can guide us toward resilience and inner peace. The Dichotomy of Control. One of the central teachings of Stoicism is the dichotomy of control. This is the idea that in life, there are things we can control and things we cannot. The Stoics urged us to focus our energy on the things that are within our control, our actions, thoughts, and emotions, while accepting that we cannot control the actions of others, the world around us, or the events that befall us. The Stoic philosopher Epictetus famously said, some things are up to us, and some things are not. By focusing on what we can control, our response is, we free ourselves from the anxiety that comes from trying to change what is beyond our reach. In practical terms, this means, focus on your reactions. You can't control other people's behavior, but you can control how you react to them. Accept the inevitable. Life is unpredictable. Accepting that setbacks and hardships are a natural part of existence allows us remain resilient when they occur. The power of perspective, cognitive reframing. Another core Stoic principle is the power of perspective. The Stoics believe that we should view every event, good or bad, with a mindset of rational detachment. It's not the events themselves that disturb us, but how we perceive them. Marcus Aurelius, one of the most famous Stoic emperors, wrote in his meditations that, the impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way. In other words, challenges are not obstacles. They are opportunities to practice virtue, to grow, and to become stronger. This concept of cognitive reframing is highly applicable in modern life. When we face a setback, rather than seeing it as a failure, we can reframe it as a lesson. When we encounter a difficult person or situation, we can use it as an opportunity to practice patience, kindness, or courage. In practical terms, this means reframe challenges. Instead of saying, this is unfair, ask, what can I learn from this situation? Shift your mindset. Try to see obstacles as stepping stones toward growth rather than roadblocks. Virtue is the highest good. For the Stoics, virtue, living a life of wisdom, courage, justice, and temperance was the highest good. They believed that living virtuously was the key to achieving inner tranquility and resilience. Everything else, whether wealth, health, or reputation, was seen as secondary. These external things can be taken away at any time, but our virtue is something that no one can take from us. The Stoics didn't view virtue as something lofty or abstract. It was something practical that we practice every day. For example, wisdom, the ability to make sound decisions and understand the nature of the world. Courage, the strength to face difficult situations with grace. Justice, acting fairly and with integrity, regardless of external circumstances. Temperance, exercising self -control and moderation, even in the face of temptation. In the modern world, this might look like acting with integrity in all situations, even when no one is watching. Facing fears with confidence, knowing that your courage is an inner strength, not tied to external validation. Maintaining balance in your life, not allowing one aspect, like work, social media, or food, to dominate. A more fatty love of fake. One of the most powerful Stoic concepts is a more fatty, which translates to love of fake. This idea teaches us to embrace everything that happens in our lives, both the good and the bad, with open arms. Instead of resisting or complaining about the circumstances we face, we are encouraged to love them and see them as essential parts of our journey. The Stoic philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche later popularized the idea of a more fatty, but it was a principle central to Stoic thought. By accepting life as it comes, without resistance or judgment, we become stronger and more resilient. In practical terms, this means embrace hardship. Instead of wishing things were different, accept them as they are and find peace in that acceptance. See obstacles as necessary. Life's difficulties are an opportunity to practice resilience, just as a weightlifter's muscles grow through resistance. How Stoicism helps us build resilience in modern times. Now that we've explored the core principles of Stoicism, let's discuss how they can help us build resilience in the modern world. Managing stress. In today's fast -paced, high -pressure world, stress is a constant companion. The Stoics remind us that while we can't always control the causes of stress, we can control how we respond to them. By practicing the dichotomy of control, we can focus our energy on what we can control, our own thoughts and actions, while letting go of the things that are beyond our influence. For example, when faced with a stressful deadline or a difficult conversation, instead of worrying about the outcome, we can focus on our preparation, our effort, and our demeanor. Navigating uncertainty. Life is filled with uncertainty, and Stoicism teaches us how to embrace it. By practicing a more fatty and viewing uncertainty as a natural part of life, we can approach the unknown with a sense of calm and confidence. This mindset allows us to act with purpose, even when the future is unclear. Overcoming setbacks, whether it's a professional failure, a personal disappointment, or a health challenge, setbacks are inevitable. The Stoic concept of perspective reminds us that setbacks are not personal affronts. They are opportunities to learn and grow. By viewing every challenge as a part of our journey, we can bounce back stronger. Stoicism teaches us that resilience isn't about avoiding hardship or controlling everything around us. It's about cultivating the inner strength to face whatever comes our way with dignity, wisdom, and grace. By embracing Stoic principles like the dichotomy of control, virtue, and a more fatty, we can become masters of our own minds and lead lives of meaning and purpose. The Stoics remind us that resilience is a choice, a mindset we can cultivate every day. It's not the world that makes us resilient. It's our response to the world that makes us strong. If you found these Stoic principles helpful and inspiring, don't forget to hit subscribe to The Unfolding Journey. Join us as we continue exploring timeless wisdom that can help you navigate the challenges of modern life with confidence, clarity, and resilience. Thanks for watching and remember your journey to inner strength and peace is just beginning.

Across the brutal Suharu Desert, these nomads survive losing a staggering 30 % of their total body weight. According to Dr. Schmidt of the Arid Lands Institute, this structural delay prevents sudden shock. Their kidneys get in on the action, too.
