Life is an unpredictable journey filled with twists, turns, and inevitable challenges. From personal setbacks to global crises, the obstacles we face can test our mental and emotional fortitude. But what if I told you that there's a way to not just survive these challenges, but to thrive in their midst? The ancient Stoics, masters of resilience, left us a treasure trove of wisdom on how to navigate life's storms with strength and grace. In this video, we're going to delve deep into how you can build unshakable resilience using Stoic practices, turning adversity into an opportunity for growth. Ready to transform your mindset? Number 1. Embrace the dichotomy of control. At the heart of Stoic resilience lies the dichotomy of control, the understanding that some things are within our control, while others are not. Epictetus, one of the most influential Stoic philosophers, taught that true freedom comes from focusing solely on what we can control, our own thoughts, actions, and attitudes. Everything else, other people's opinions, external events, or the outcomes of our efforts, is beyond our control and should be accepted as such. When you internalize this principle, you free yourself from the unnecessary stress and anxiety that come from trying to control the uncontrollable. This mental shift not only reduces the emotional burden of adversity, but also empowers you to take meaningful action where it matters most. Imagine you're facing a major challenge at work, such as an unexpected project deadline. Instead of stressing over how others will perceive your work or whether the project will succeed, focus on what you can control, your effort, your organization, and your response to the pressure. By directing your energy toward these controllable factors, factors, you build resilience by enhancing your ability to navigate stress and uncertainty. To reinforce this mindset, practice regularly distinguishing between what is and isn't within your control. For every challenge you face, make a list of the factors you can influence and those you cannot. Commit to focusing only on the former. Over time, this practice will strengthen your resilience, as you'll become adept at letting go of what you can't change and directing your efforts toward what you can. Number 2. Reframe adversity as opportunity. One of the most powerful Stoic practices for building resilience is the art of reframing. Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher, taught that the impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way. This Stoic maxim encourages us to view obstacles not as insurmountable barriers, but as opportunities to grow, learn, and improve. When you encounter adversity, the initial reaction might be frustration or despair. However, by consciously reframing the situation, you can transform your perspective. Instead of asking, why is this happening to me? Ask, what can I learn from this? How can this make me stronger? This shift in mindset allows you to see challenges as valuable experiences that contribute to your personal growth and resilience. For example, if you experience a personal setback, such as a failed relationship, rather than dwelling on the pain, consider what the experience has taught you about yourself, your needs, and your boundaries. Use these insights to improve future relationships and to grow as an individual. This reframing not only eases the emotional impact of the setback, but also builds resilience by empowering you to turn adversity into an opportunity for self -improvement. Whenever you face a challenge, make a conscious effort to reframe it in a positive light. Write down the lessons you can learn and the ways in which the experience can help you grow. By consistently practicing this reframing technique, you'll train your mind to automatically see obstacles as opportunities, thereby enhancing your resilience. Number 3. Practice negative visualization. Negative visualization is a core stoic exercise that involves imagining potential difficulties or worst -case scenarios before they happen. While it might seem counterintuitive to dwell on negative outcomes, this practice actually serves to prepare your mind for adversity, making you less susceptible to being overwhelmed when challenges arise. Seneca, one of the great stoic thinkers, recommended regularly reflecting on the possibility of loss, hardship, or failure. This doesn't mean living in a state of constant worry, but rather familiarizing yourself with the possibility of difficult situations so that, if they do occur, you're mentally prepared to handle them with calm and composure. For instance, if you're about to embark on a significant career change, spend some time considering what could go wrong. Perhaps the new job isn't what you expected, or you face unforeseen challenges in adapting to a new role. By visualizing these potential difficulties, you build resilience by reducing the element of surprise and by mentally preparing strategies to cope with them. When adversity strikes, you're less likely to be caught off guard and more likely to respond with clarity and confidence. Incorporate negative visualization into your daily or weekly routine. Spend a few minutes imagining potential challenges or setbacks in your life. Consider how you would respond and what actions you could take to mitigate their impact. This mental rehearsal strengthens your resilience by equipping you with the foresight and preparedness to face adversity calmly and effectively. Number four, cultivate emotional detachment. Emotional detachment, or apathia, is a stoic practice that involves maintaining a sense of inner calm and equilibrium, regardless of external circumstances. The Stoics believed that while we cannot control what happens to us, we can control our emotional reactions to those events. By cultivating emotional detachment, we build resilience by not allowing our emotions to dictate our actions or overwhelm our rational thinking. This doesn't mean suppressing your emotions or becoming indifferent to life's challenges. Instead, it's about observing your emotions without letting them control you. When you face adversity, practice stepping back and viewing the situation objectively. Recognize the emotions that arise, but choose not to be ruled by them. This detachment allows you to respond to challenges with a clear mind and balanced judgment. For example, if you receive harsh criticism, instead of reacting defensively or letting it affect your self -esteem, practice emotional detachment. Acknowledge the initial sting of the criticism, but then assess it calmly and rationally. Is there any truth to the feedback? If so, use it as an opportunity to improve. If not, let it go. By not allowing your emotions to dictate your response, you build the resilience to handle criticism and other emotional triggers with grace. When you encounter an emotionally charged situation, take a few deep breaths and consciously separate yourself from the emotion. Imagine that you're an observer watching the situation unfold without getting personally involved. This practice helps you maintain emotional detachment, which strengthens your resilience by enabling you to navigate challenges with a calm and composed mindset. Number five, practice self -discipline and voluntary discomfort. Resilience is not just a mental or emotional trait. It's also a matter of physical and behavioral discipline. The Stoics believed that self -discipline is key to building resilience. And one of the ways they practiced this was through voluntary discomfort, deliberately exposing themselves to hardship in order to strengthen their character. By engaging in practices that challenge your physical and mental comfort, you train yourself to endure discomfort without complaint. This builds resilience by making you more adaptable and less reliant on external comforts. When real adversity strikes, you're better prepared to handle it because you've already conditioned yourself to face challenges with strength and determination. For example, the Stoics might practice fasting, take cold baths, or engage in strenuous physical exercise as a way to toughen themselves up. You can apply this principle in your own life by incorporating similar practices. Try intermittent fasting, taking cold showers, or pushing yourself in your workouts. These small acts of voluntary discomfort help you build resilience by teaching you to embrace challenges and discomfort as opportunities to grow stronger. Choose one or two practices of voluntary discomfort to incorporate into your daily routine. Whether it's fasting, cold exposure, or challenging physical exercise, commit to pushing your limits regularly. Over time, these practices will build your physical and mental resilience, making you more capable of handling life's inevitable difficulties. Number six, develop a strong sense of purpose. A clear sense of purpose is a powerful motivator and a key component of resilience. The Stoics believe that living in alignment with your values and purpose was essential for enduring and overcoming life's challenges. When you have a strong sense of purpose, you're more likely to persevere through adversity because you're driven by something greater than yourself. Purpose gives meaning to your efforts and helps you maintain perspective during tough times. When challenges arise, they don't seem as daunting because they're part of a larger mission. This sense of purpose acts as an anchor, keeping you grounded and focused no matter what obstacles you face. For example, if your purpose is to contribute to your community, challenges like personal setbacks or professional difficulties may feel less overwhelming because they are framed within the context of your broader mission. Your sense of purpose gives you the resilience to keep moving forward, even when the road is tough. Take time to reflect on your core values and what drives you. Write down your life's purpose and revisit it regularly, especially when you're facing challenges. Let this sense of purpose guide your actions and decisions. By aligning your life with your purpose, you build resilience by ensuring that your efforts are always directed towards something meaningful and fulfilling. Number seven, engage in regular reflection and journaling. Reflection and journaling are vital practices for building resilience. The Stoics, including Marcus Aurelius, were ardent practitioners of journaling, using it as a tool to reflect on their thoughts, actions, and experiences. By regularly engaging in reflection, you gain insights into your behaviors, learn from your mistakes, and reinforce your commitment to Stoic principles. Journaling allows you to process your experiences and emotions, providing clarity and perspective. When you reflect on your day, you can identify areas where you exhibited resilience and areas where you can improve. This self -awareness is crucial for growth and for building the mental and emotional resilience to face future challenges. For instance, if you encounter a difficult situation, write about it in your journal. Reflect on how you handled it, what you learned, and how you can apply these lessons moving forward. This practice not only helps you process your emotions, but also reinforces your ability to navigate similar challenges in the future. Set aside time each day or week for journaling and reflection. Use this time to review your experiences, assess your responses to challenges, and plan how to apply Stoic principles more effectively in your life. Regular journaling builds resilience by fostering a deeper understanding of yourself and by reinforcing your commitment to personal growth and Stoic practices. The Stoics believed that one of the fundamental truths of life is its impermanence. Everything, whether it's joy, sorrow, success, or failure, is temporary. By embracing the impermanence of all things, you can build resilience by learning to detach from the highs and lows of life and by maintaining a balanced perspective. This principle helps you navigate adversity with greater ease because you understand that no situation, no matter how difficult, will last forever. By accepting the transient nature of life's events, you reduce the emotional weight of challenges and develop the resilience to endure them with grace. For example, if you're going through a tough time, remind yourself that this too shall pass. Reflect on past difficulties that you've overcome and how they eventually resolved. This mindset helps you build resilience by fostering a calm and accepting attitude toward life's inevitable ups and downs. In moments of stress or difficulty, take a step back and remind yourself of the impermanence of all things. Reflect on how this situation is just one chapter in the larger story of your life. Reflect practice builds resilience by helping you maintain a balanced perspective and by reducing the emotional impact of temporary challenges. Number 9. Led by example and practice Stoic virtues. The Stoics taught that resilience is closely tied to living a life of virtue. By embodying the core Stoic virtues, wisdom, courage, justice, and temperance, you build the moral foundation necessary to face adversity with integrity and strength. When you lead by example, you not only strengthen your own resilience but also inspire others to do the same. Living virtuously gives you the inner strength to withstand challenges, knowing that you are acting in alignment with your values. Whether you are facing a difficult decision or dealing with a personal setback, practicing Stoic virtues helps you stay grounded and resilient. For instance, if you are in a challenging situation at work, apply the virtue of wisdom by carefully considering your options, courage by taking the right action despite fear, and justice by ensuring fairness in your decisions. This virtuous approach builds resilience by reinforcing your commitment to what is right, no matter the obstacles you face. Make a conscious effort to practice Stoic virtues in your daily life. Reflect on how you can embody wisdom, courage, justice, and temperance in your actions and decisions. By consistently practicing these virtues, you build resilience by aligning your life with your values, and by strengthening your inner resolve to face challenges with integrity. Number 10. Cultivate gratitude and focus on what you have. Finally, the Stoics believed that cultivating gratitude is essential for resilience. By focusing on what you have rather than what you lack, you develop a sense of contentment and inner peace, which strengthens your ability to cope with adversity. Gratitude shifts your perspective from what is missing in your life to what is present, helping you maintain a positive outlook even in difficult times. When you practice gratitude, you remind yourself of the abundance in your life, no matter how small. This mindset helps you build resilience by reducing the impact of challenges, and by reinforcing your ability to find joy and satisfaction in the present moment. For example, if you're facing financial difficulties, focus on what you still have, your health, your relationships, or even the simple pleasures of life. This practice not only reduces the stress of the situation, but also builds resilience by fostering a sense of contentment and inner strength. Incorporate a daily gratitude practice into your routine. Each day, take a few moments to reflect on and appreciate the positive aspects of your life. By consistently focusing on what you have, you build resilience by nurturing a mindset of abundance and contentment, which helps you navigate life's challenges with greater ease. Thank you for joining me on this journey into the heart of Stoic resilience. By embracing these timeless practices, you can develop the inner strength to face life's challenges with grace, courage, and wisdom. Remember, resilience isn't just about enduring hardship. It's about growing stronger through it. If you found this video helpful, don't forget to like, share, and subscribe for more insights on living a Stoic life. Together, let's continue our pursuit of resilience, inner peace, and a life well lived. Until next time, stay strong and stay Stoic.
sources.title: How to Build Resilience with Stoic Practices

[SPEAKER_00]
Have you ever wondered what makes Generation Z so different? It's a question that continues to pique our curiosity, sparking debates and discussions around the world. Born from the mid -90s to the early 2000s, Generation Z is the group succeeding the Millennials, making up a significant portion of the global population. As the first generation to grow up with the Internet and smartphones in their hands, they're unlike any group that's come before them. Their unique experiences and perspectives have led to a fascinating array of psychological traits that set them apart. Understanding these traits isn't just about keeping up with the latest trends or buzzwords. It's about recognizing the forces that are shaping our society and our future. It's about gaining insights into the minds of those who are, right now, stepping onto the world stage and making their voices heard. So brace yourself as we dive into the intriguing world of Generation Z. Can you imagine a world without the Internet, smartphones or social media? Generation Z can't. They are the true digital natives because they grew up during the era of rapid technological advancement. They have never known a time before having Google at their fingertips, being instantly connected through social media, or having access to countless books and articles through the Internet. This constant interaction with technology has profoundly shaped their communication styles, learning methods, and thought processes. Consider communication. Smartphones are more than tools for the members of Generation Z. They are extensions of their identities. They use them to express their feelings, share their experiences, and connect with others around the globe. They've swapped handwritten letters for instant messages and face -to -face meetings for video chats. They've even developed a language of their own, one that's filled with emojis, memes, and abbreviations. In terms of learning methods, Generation Z has grown up with the world's knowledge at their fingertips. They're accustomed to seeking out information online, be it through educational platforms, YouTube tutorials, or even social media. This has made them self -directed learners, who are not only comfortable with technology, but also expect it to be part of their educational experience. And let's not forget about their thought processes. Being constantly connected has led Generation Z to develop an always -on mentality. They're used to quick responses, instant gratification, and a constant flow of information. This has made them efficient problem solvers and quick decision makers. However, it has also made them more prone to distractions and less patient with delays. Thus, being digital natives, Generation Z has a unique way of interacting with the world. They're reshaping the norms of communication, redefining the methods of learning, and rethinking the ways we process information. Their digital fluency is not just a characteristic, it's a fundamental part of their identity. And as they continue to grow and influence the world, understanding this digital DNA is key to understanding Generation Z. Ever seen someone text, watch a video, and do homework all at once? That's a typical Gen Z multitasker. The ability to multitask is a real strength of the Z generation. As digital natives, they are used to having a lot of distractions vying for their focus. This has produced a generation that is extraordinarily skilled at multitasking, able to switch gears from one activity to another with the grace of a well -choreographed dance. Think about the typical day of a member of Generation Z. They could be researching for a school project while simultaneously texting a friend and watching their favorite show online streaming service. They can be engaged in a video conference for a group assignment, yet still find time to scroll through their social media feeds and respond to comments. Their ability to switch between tasks is akin to having several browser tabs open, each of which represents a different project. This multitasking ability is not just about being productive or efficient. It's also about navigating a world where information overload is the norm. For Gen Z, multitasking is a survival skill, a way to sift through the flood of information and stimuli that come their way every day. Despite the benefits, though, multitasking does have negative effects on attention and presence that must be taken into account. While members of Generation Z may be multitasking experts, that does not mean they are focusing on each task equally. Doing a lot and doing it well are two different things. Too much multitasking can lead to a lack of focus, which can affect the quality of their work and their ability to be fully present in any given moment. The ability to focus, to give one's undivided attention to a single task, is equally important. It's about depth over breadth, quality over quantity. It's about being in the moment, fully engaged and immersed in what you're doing. While multitasking is a remarkable Gen Z trait, the importance of focused attention should not be overlooked. Gen Z is not just observing the world, they're actively participating in reshaping it. This generation is characterized by a heightened sense of social consciousness, a deep commitment to social justice, and a fervent dedication to environmental issues. They are not content to sit on the sidelines, passively watching as the world evolves. Instead, they are stepping up, taking action, and making a tangible difference. Gen Z's concern for social justice is deeply ingrained. They are not just aware of the inequality and injustice that exist in the world. They are actively working to challenge and change these societal norms. Whether it's marching in a protest, launching a social media campaign, or volunteering their time and resources, Gen Z is determined to make the world a fairer and more just place. Their commitment to environmental issues is equally impressive. Raised in an era of climate change and environmental degradation, Gen Z is leading the charge in advocating for sustainable solutions. They're pushing for renewable energy, advocating for waste reduction, and promoting sustainable living. They're not just thinking about their future, they're actively working to protect it. Gen Z's commitment to social justice and environmental sustainability is not a passing trend or a marketing gimmick. It's a deeply held belief, a core part of their identity. They're not just talking about change, they're living it, breathing it, and making it happen. With their strong social conscience, Generation Z is truly a generation of changemakers. Waiting for opportunities? Not Generation Z. They're creating them. This spirited generation of self -starters is redefining the meaning of initiative. They're not idly sitting by, passively waiting for doors to open. Instead, they're actively seeking out opportunities and, when necessary, building their own doors. This entrepreneurial spirit is deeply rooted in Generation Z's psyche, and it's driven by a couple of key factors. The first is their desire for financial stability. In a world that's constantly changing, where economic certainty seems more like a myth than a reality, Gen Z is taking matters into their own hands. They're starting businesses, creating apps, launching social movements, and so much more, all in an effort to secure their financial future. The second factor is their passion for making a difference. Generation Z is not content with just making money. They want their work to have an impact. They're driven by purpose and the desire to bring about positive change in the world. This is evident in the types of businesses they're starting, businesses that are socially responsible, environmentally friendly, and community -focused. So what does this all mean? It means that Generation Z is a generation of doers. They're proactive, ambitious, and they're not afraid to take risks. They're creating their own paths, shaping their own futures, and in the process, they're changing the world. Generation Z, with their entrepreneurial spirit, are indeed the architects of their own destiny. Generation Z has faced significant challenges, but guess what? They've shown remarkable resilience. From the global pandemic to social unrest, this generation has dealt with the sort of upheavals that could easily shake anyone to their core. Yet, they've handled it with grace and tenacity. Remember, resilience isn't about avoiding difficulties. It's about bouncing back from them, and Gen Z has this down to a science. They've shown us that they can adapt, change, and grow in the face of adversity, embodying the very essence of resilience. They're resourceful, employing new ways to learn, communicate, and live in a rapidly changing world. This is not a generation that hides from challenges or shies away from the tough stuff. Instead, they meet it head -on, using their unique blend of digital savviness, multitasking abilities, social consciousness, and entrepreneurial spirit to navigate their way through. Despite the hurdles, Generation Z continues to shine with their resilience. So, we've explored the five key psychological traits that define Generation Z. They are the digital natives, born into a world where technology is as natural as breathing. They're multitaskers, juggling digital tasks with ease, yet learning to be present in the moment. They're socially conscious, ready to roll up their sleeves and make a difference in the world. They exhibit an entrepreneurial spirit, creating opportunities instead of waiting for them. And finally, resilience defines them. They've faced adversity head -on and have shown an impressive ability to adapt and overcome. These traits not only define Generation Z, but they also shape our world, both now and in the future. As we continue to understand this generation better, we can't help but see their influence everywhere. We'd love to hear our thoughts on today's topic. Feel free to share in the comment section below. And if you found this subject to be enlightening, feel free to give us a like, share it with your friends, and subscribe to Noggin Knowledge for more psychology insights every week. Until next time, take care, stay aware, and keep growing.

[None]
Thank you. Thank you.

Cockroaches are the ultimate survivors of the animal kingdom. Imagine an insect so resilient that it thrived alongside dinosaurs and continued to flourish even after an asteroid wiped out nearly all life on Earth. While most species succumbed to the harsh aftermath, these tiny creatures endured and adapted, earning their reputation as some of nature's most indestructible organisms. Today, cockroaches remain a fascinating symbol of survival, thriving in environments as diverse as tropical jungles and bustling cities. Cockroaches first appeared over 300 million years ago, during the Carboniferous Period, a time when Earth's landscapes were dominated by vast swamps and towering vegetation. These ancient cockroaches were larger than today's species and roamed dense forests teeming with life. Their design has remained relatively unchanged, a testament to their evolutionary success. Long before dinosaurs walked the Earth, cockroaches had already established themselves as adaptable and resourceful survivors. This head start allowed them to endure through the rise and fall of some of history's most formidable creatures. The physical features of cockroaches are perfectly designed for survival. Their tough yet flexible exoskeleton provides a protective shield against predators and injuries, while allowing them to squeeze into the narrowest cracks to escape danger or find shelter. Their six powerful legs give them remarkable speed and agility, helping them evade even the quickest of attackers. Perhaps most impressive is their ability to survive on virtually anything. Cockroaches are not picky eaters. They can thrive on decaying plant matter, glue, soap and even cardboard. This resourcefulness has allowed them to adapt to a variety of environments, from ancient forests to modern human homes. Sixty -six million years ago, a massive asteroid struck the Earth, triggering a catastrophic chain of events that caused the extinction of nearly 75 % of life on the planet, including the dinosaurs. But cockroaches endured. Their small, flat bodies allowed them to hide in cracks and crevices, protecting them from the immediate impacts of fire and ash. Unlike larger animals that struggled to find food, cockroaches could survive on tiny scraps of organic material. Their minimal oxygen requirements also helped them endure during a time when the atmosphere was choked with debris. These traits allowed cockroaches to navigate and thrive through one of Earth's most devastating mass extinction events. Cockroaches Cockroaches Cockroaches ensured their survival not just through their physical traits, but also with their ingenious reproductive strategies. Female cockroaches produce egg cases known as utheci, which act like tiny protective capsules. These utheci shield their eggs from predators, extreme weather, and other threats, significantly increasing the likelihood of their offspring's survival. This adaptation allowed cockroach populations to persist and even thrive in conditions that would have wiped out less resilient species. By protecting their next generation so effectively, cockroaches secured their place in the evolutionary timeline. Cockroaches possess survival traits that seem almost superhuman. They can go for weeks without food, thanks to their low energy requirements, and can survive for several days without water. Even more astonishing is their ability to live for days without their heads. Without their head, cockroaches continue functioning until they eventually die from dehydration, not injury. These traits make cockroaches incredibly difficult to eliminate, contributing to their reputation as one of the toughest creatures on the planet. One of the most remarkable aspects of cockroaches is their ability to adapt to nearly every environment on Earth. They have evolved to live in deserts, tropical jungles, and even freezing mountain regions. Today, there are over 4,500 species of cockroaches, and only about 30 are considered pests that coexist closely with humans. The rest thrive in the wild, where they play essential roles in ecosystems. Their adaptability has allowed them to inhabit nearly every continent and environment, making them one of the most widespread insects in the world. Despite their reputation as pests, cockroaches are essential players in their ecosystems. They act as decomposers, breaking down organic material and recycling nutrients back into the soil. This process helps maintain healthy ecosystems and supports plant growth. In the natural world, cockroaches contribute to the balance of life, serving as food for other creatures and playing a vital role in nutrient cycles. While their presence in human spaces can be unwelcome, their role in nature is undeniably important. From prehistoric forests to modern urban jungles, cockroaches have proven themselves to be unparalleled survivors. Their resilience, adaptability, and ingenuity have allowed them to endure the harshest conditions and outlive some of history's most powerful creatures. Whether you admire them or feel uneasy around them, there's no denying that cockroaches are a testament to the incredible power of nature's design. They remind us of the strength that comes with adaptability and the will to survive against all odds. And we'll see you next time.

Deal Highlights - NQS (National Quality Systems)
Founded by multi-time entrepreneur Mark Feinberg, NQS is a vertical AI platform designed to streamline trauma registry management for hospital emergency departments. The company addresses a highly specialized domestic market of approximately 2,400 trauma registry departments—a space previously served by a single, broad-based incumbent whose undifferentiated software left users deeply underserved.
11 Tribes co-invested alongside lead investor Long Run Capital, committing an initial $750,000 check into a priced seed round at an $8 million post-money valuation, with the total raise of $2 million split between the two firms. A defining feature of the investment was NQS's 16 signed hospital contracts at the time of closing—despite the product being six to eight weeks from launch—a rare validation of both market urgency and founder credibility.
Operating partner Carolyn Wilson, former COO of the University of Chicago Health System, provided critical domain expertise during diligence. The round closed in March 2025, the product launched within weeks, and NQS has since grown rapidly. 11 Tribes has made two additional investment tranches, including a recent $750,000 follow-on that effectively constitutes a Series A.

Every founder has a season they leave out of the story. The stretch where the company almost went under. The years of doubt, failure, and quiet identity crisis that never make it into the profile piece.
Through the Valley is a long-form interview show about those chapters. Host Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, sits down with founders and leaders to talk honestly about what it cost to get here, and who they became on the way through.

Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout.
What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die.
Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born.
In this episode:
• What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair
• The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working
• Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness
• The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time
• How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today
• Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it
• What he would say to himself on the worst night in the valley

Pro Basketball to 5x Founder: A Masterclass in Resilience | Jordan Fliegel
At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement.
He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now.
Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him.
In this episode:
The napkin math that shows exactly when your investors' incentives stop matching yours
Why he ran through Boston in tears to a mentor's office with no appointment
What it feels like to sit in meetings where every good idea you offer undermines your own successor
How he told ten employees the money was gone, and what he had to say to the one he couldn't save
The letter his mentor wrote him, read out loud for the first time
Why he took a company from "we can't pay our bills" to a $48M exit
The Jocko Willink rule he now applies to every piece of bad news

Cancer at 30, and the Company He Built After It | Founder Brandon Aversano, The Alloy Market
In the fall of 2022 Brandon Aversano was 30 years old, away on a trip in California, and found it himself in the middle of the night. Thirty minutes after an ultrasound the chief of urology walked into the room and told him there was a 99% chance it was testicular cancer. His first thought wasn’t about himself. It was how he was going to tell his mom.
Nothing could be known before surgery. Three weeks of sitting with whether it was in one spot or everywhere. His dad had prostate cancer the year before. Brandon had built an identity on competence, distinguished scholar, Deloitte, JetBlue, JP Morgan, and the one thing he suddenly couldn’t do was be the capable one. He went on disability the day after scheduling surgery and had free time for the first time in a decade.
Mark Phillips sits with Brandon on what that season cost and what it built: the medical debt that horrified a father who hated debt, the trip to Jewelers Row with his grandmother’s jewelry where strangers offered twenty cents on the dollar, the 401k he emptied into a company, the $40,000 mobile app his co-founder told him to scrap, and the surgeon who said the book on whether it comes back is already written and he doesn’t get to read the last chapter for five years.

- What three weeks of not knowing does to someone who built his life on competence

Why There's Shame in Getting Sober but None in the Damage | With The Maze Founder Justin Gurland
Justin Gurland arrived at rehab at eleven at night, three thousand miles from everyone he knew. He woke up the next morning in Los Angeles on Super Bowl Sunday, 2008, gave himself the finger in the mirror, and watched the Giants beat the undefeated Patriots. Then the staff turned off the game, walked everyone into a group room, and asked what each of them believed in.
He was twenty-five. He had no community, no sober person anywhere in his life to point at, and no idea what the question meant. What he said was that the Giants had just won and he could hold on to that for now. He describes the moment as meaningless on its face, a football game, a team he wasn't on. It was also the only thing he had.
Mark Phillips sits with Justin eighteen years later, five blocks from The Maze, the members club he opened in the Flatiron where hundreds of New Yorkers pay to belong to a building with no alcohol in it. They talk about the sister who told him she couldn't take it anymore, the letter his father hand-wrote for this episode, the Grateful Dead lyric he keeps returning to, and the question he still can't answer: why the shame attaches to getting sober instead of to the damage.
In this episode:
• Why he says his sister saved his life, and what happens to people who never get that conversation
• The Godfather scene he read a month before everything came apart, and why it stayed with him
• What he actually said when a counselor asked the room about God
• Playing a kids' board game in treatment and feeling his side hurt from laughing for the first time in years
• What his father wrote about Justin's lowest moment, and where his relationship with him sits now
• Why there is shame in getting sober and none in the harm that came before it
• The alcohol-free movement he did not know existed until it was growing in front of him
• What he would say if he could sit with himself on the worst night: take this in, and get to work

Why Brutal Honesty Is the Kindest Thing an Investor Can Do, with VC Coach Charlie O’Donnell
For 20 years, Charlie O'Donnell was the most findable investor in New York. Email on the front page of his site, pitch me anything, come to the dinner. Then in May 2023 he wrote a sentence announcing his last venture deal and stopped.
The market didn't push him out. Most people in venture keep raising because it's a good job and there's always a next fund. Charlie ran Brooklyn Bridge Ventures as a solo first-check investor across more than 100 companies, and when he looked at the two available ways to keep doing it into his 40s (hire a younger version of himself, or stop looking at anything pre-revenue) he decided he'd rather not do the job at all than do it that way.
Mark Phillips sits with Charlie on what it costs to hold a career loosely: the ice cream shop that went to zero and the conversation he never had with those founders, the marathon he ran badly and blamed on the wind, the 80 days in the NICU where three term sheets got signed, and the firefighter father who played tennis in the morning and did tax returns in the afternoon and was content.
In this episode:
• Why Charlie stopped raising funds while the option to continue was still open
• The tradeoff he now tells every founder about before they take a check
• How to hold "good investor" as a job rather than an identity

From Losing Everything at 30 to Building the Firm That Coaches Fortune 100 Executives: Jason Jaggard
Jason Jaggard is the founder of Novus Global, one of the biggest executive coaching firms in the world whose coaches work with Global Executives, professional athletes, and Grammy-winning artists. But at 30, his life collapsed. In a single year, he quit a great job, lost 90% of his revenue, and watched his most important relationship fall apart. We talk about what broke, why it broke, and how that year became the foundation for the firm he leads today.
In this first episode of Through the Valley, Jason talks with Mark Phillips about the night he collapsed on his apartment floor, the "cold war" he entered with God, and how the tools he found in his darkest season became the foundation of a coaching firm that now serves some of the most influential leaders on Earth.
They cover why blame keeps you stuck, why self-pity is a drug, the difference between psychological safety and psychological strength, and why community is the closest thing to a bulletproof vest a founder can wear.
Through the Valley is hosted by Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, and explores the seasons of loss, failure, and doubt behind remarkable careers.

What is acquisition entrepreneurship? It is the practice of searching for and buying established, profitable small businesses - usually from a retiring owner. Fruition Capital invests in these businesses.
I invited Jason Ehrlich, Managing Partner of Fruition Capital on ATLalts to discuss why he believes investing in the acquisition of small businesses can allow investors to take advantage of what he believes are four key factors:
Generational transfer of US small businesses owned by Baby Boomers is underway. Greater then 3 million profitable businesses owned by 65+ year-old owners will change hands in the next 5-10 yearsAttractive acquisition prices of 3x-5x avg. acquisition multiples (of EBITDA) for target businesses.Probability of failure is low as only 2.1% of SBA 7a Business Acquisition Loans defaulted in 2023The Chance of attractive performance is high as 75% of sesarch entrepreneur investors achieved an IRR of 20% according to one study.
Jason Ehrlich, Managing Partner of Fruition Capital, discusses how his firm focuses on investing in B2B companies with stable earnings and a repeat customer base, which he refers to as "enduring profitability." Ehrlich also elaborates on the unique structure of Fruition Capital, which differentiates itself by partnering closely with entrepreneurs while providing significant capital and operational support. As the discussion progresses, Sreeni delves into the current economic landscape, noting the potential for fixed-income investments amid declining interest rates and controlled inflation. The conversation underscores the significance of education in the financial sector, with Sreeni advocating for transparency and trust-building between Angel Oak and its clients. Through The Valley
Mark Phillips
0.0 (0)
Emprendimiento
Cada semana
Every founder has a season they leave out of the story. The stretch where the company almost went under. The years of doubt, failure, and quiet identity crisis that never make it into the profile piece.
Through the Valley is a long-form interview show about those chapters. Host Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, sits down with founders and leaders to talk honestly about what it cost to get here, and who they became on the way through.
New episodes every Wednesday.
Episodio más reciente
Del más reciente al más antiguo
Del más antiguo al más reciente

hace 4 días
Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout. What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die. Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born. In this episode: • What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair • The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working • Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness • The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time • How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today • Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it • What he would say to himself on the worst night in the valley Subscribe to Through the Valley wherever you listen. New episodes on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Find Michael at lonelyentrepreneur.com. 48 min
16 sep
Pro Basketball to 5x Founder: A Masterclass in Resilience | Jordan Fliegel
At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement. He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now. Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him. In this episode: The napkin math that shows exactly when your investors' incentives stop matching yoursWhy he ran through Boston in tears to a mentor's office with no appointmentWhat it feels like to sit in meetings where every good idea you offer undermines your own successorHow he told ten employees the money was gone, and what he had to say to the one he couldn't saveThe letter his mentor wrote him, read out loud for the first timeWhy he took a company from "we can't pay our bills" to a $48M exitThe Jocko Willink rule he now applies to every piece of bad news Subscribe for new episodes of Through the Valley every week. Watch on YouTube, listen on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Cancer at 30, and the Company He Built After It | Founder Brandon Aversano, The Alloy Market
In the fall of 2022 Brandon Aversano was 30 years old, away on a trip in California, and found it himself in the middle of the night. Thirty minutes after an ultrasound the chief of urology walked into the room and told him there was a 99% chance it was testicular cancer. His first thought wasn’t about himself. It was how he was going to tell his mom. Nothing could be known before surgery. Three weeks of sitting with whether it was in one spot or everywhere. His dad had prostate cancer the year before. Brandon had built an identity on competence, distinguished scholar, Deloitte, JetBlue, JP Morgan, and the one thing he suddenly couldn’t do was be the capable one. He went on disability the day after scheduling surgery and had free time for the first time in a decade. Mark Phillips sits with Brandon on what that season cost and what it built: the medical debt that horrified a father who hated debt, the trip to Jewelers Row with his grandmother’s jewelry where strangers offered twenty cents on the dollar, the 401k he emptied into a company, the $40,000 mobile app his co-founder told him to scrap, and the surgeon who said the book on whether it comes back is already written and he doesn’t get to read the last chapter for five years. In this episode: - The 24 hours between finding it himself and hearing the number - Why telling his parents was harder than hearing the diagnosis - What three weeks of not knowing does to someone who built his life on competence - Jewelers Row, twenty cents on the dollar, and the moment Alloy became obvious - The customer who asked to speak to the founder and had them both crying on the phone - Learning to control the controllable, and the chapter he doesn’t get to read for five years - The letter from a friend of eighteen years, and what he’d tell himself on the worst night Subscribe to Through the Valley on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Brandon’s company, The Alloy Market, sends a free evaluation kit to anyone looking to sell gold. Why There's Shame in Getting Sober but None in the Damage | With The Maze Founder Justin Gurland
Justin Gurland arrived at rehab at eleven at night, three thousand miles from everyone he knew. He woke up the next morning in Los Angeles on Super Bowl Sunday, 2008, gave himself the finger in the mirror, and watched the Giants beat the undefeated Patriots. Then the staff turned off the game, walked everyone into a group room, and asked what each of them believed in. He was twenty-five. He had no community, no sober person anywhere in his life to point at, and no idea what the question meant. What he said was that the Giants had just won and he could hold on to that for now. He describes the moment as meaningless on its face, a football game, a team he wasn't on. It was also the only thing he had. Mark Phillips sits with Justin eighteen years later, five blocks from The Maze, the members club he opened in the Flatiron where hundreds of New Yorkers pay to belong to a building with no alcohol in it. They talk about the sister who told him she couldn't take it anymore, the letter his father hand-wrote for this episode, the Grateful Dead lyric he keeps returning to, and the question he still can't answer: why the shame attaches to getting sober instead of to the damage. In this episode: • Why he says his sister saved his life, and what happens to people who never get that conversation • The Godfather scene he read a month before everything came apart, and why it stayed with him • What he actually said when a counselor asked the room about God • Playing a kids' board game in treatment and feeling his side hurt from laughing for the first time in years • What his father wrote about Justin's lowest moment, and where his relationship with him sits now • Why there is shame in getting sober and none in the harm that came before it • The alcohol-free movement he did not know existed until it was growing in front of him • What he would say if he could sit with himself on the worst night: take this in, and get to work Subscribe to Through the Valley on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. You can find The Maze at themazenyc.com, on Instagram at @themazenyc, and on LinkedIn. Why Brutal Honesty Is the Kindest Thing an Investor Can Do, with VC Coach Charlie O’Donnell
For 20 years, Charlie O'Donnell was the most findable investor in New York. Email on the front page of his site, pitch me anything, come to the dinner. Then in May 2023 he wrote a sentence announcing his last venture deal and stopped. The market didn't push him out. Most people in venture keep raising because it's a good job and there's always a next fund. Charlie ran Brooklyn Bridge Ventures as a solo first-check investor across more than 100 companies, and when he looked at the two available ways to keep doing it into his 40s (hire a younger version of himself, or stop looking at anything pre-revenue) he decided he'd rather not do the job at all than do it that way. Mark Phillips sits with Charlie on what it costs to hold a career loosely: the ice cream shop that went to zero and the conversation he never had with those founders, the marathon he ran badly and blamed on the wind, the 80 days in the NICU where three term sheets got signed, and the firefighter father who played tennis in the morning and did tax returns in the afternoon and was content. In this episode: • Why Charlie stopped raising funds while the option to continue was still open • The tradeoff he now tells every founder about before they take a check • How to hold "good investor" as a job rather than an identity • What 16 collapsed triathletes reveal about experienced high performers • The rounded-up revenue number that quietly ends a fundraise • What his father's illness taught him about asking what a person actually needs • The one thing he realized far too late about being a partner at home Subscribe to Through the Valley on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Charlie's book, Founder Unfriendly: What Investors Won't Tell You About Getting Funded, is available wherever you buy books, and his newsletter has been running at thisisgoingtobebig.com since 2004.
52 min
18 ago
From Losing Everything at 30 to Building the Firm That Coaches Fortune 100 Executives: Jason Jaggard
Jason Jaggard is the founder of Novus Global, one of the biggest executive coaching firms in the world whose coaches work with Global Executives, professional athletes, and Grammy-winning artists. But at 30, his life collapsed. In a single year, he quit a great job, lost 90% of his revenue, and watched his most important relationship fall apart. We talk about what broke, why it broke, and how that year became the foundation for the firm he leads today. In this first episode of Through the Valley, Jason talks with Mark Phillips about the night he collapsed on his apartment floor, the "cold war" he entered with God, and how the tools he found in his darkest season became the foundation of a coaching firm that now serves some of the most influential leaders on Earth. They cover why blame keeps you stuck, why self-pity is a drug, the difference between psychological safety and psychological strength, and why community is the closest thing to a bulletproof vest a founder can wear. Through the Valley is hosted by Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, and explores the seasons of loss, failure, and doubt behind remarkable careers. Impact Investing Roadshow
56m
Mark Phillips, Founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, joins Impact Investing Roadshow to discuss his firm's founder-first venture capital thesis and their investment in NQS (National Quality Systems), a vertical AI platform transforming trauma registry management for U.S. hospital emergency departments.
Get The Full Episode Notes Here
Mark Phillips
Founder, 11 Tribes Ventures
Email | LinkedIn | Website
Masters of Resilience Podcast | Co-hosted Mark Phillips and Ryan Seger
Deal Highlights - NQS (National Quality Systems)
Founded by multi-time entrepreneur Mark Feinberg, NQS is a vertical AI platform designed to streamline trauma registry management for hospital emergency departments. The company addresses a highly specialized domestic market of approximately 2,400 trauma registry departments—a space previously served by a single, broad-based incumbent whose undifferentiated software left users deeply underserved.
11 Tribes co-invested alongside lead investor Long Run Capital, committing an initial $750,000 check into a priced seed round at an $8 million post-money valuation, with the total raise of $2 million split between the two firms. A defining feature of the investment was NQS's 16 signed hospital contracts at the time of closing—despite the product being six to eight weeks from launch—a rare validation of both market urgency and founder credibility.
Operating partner Carolyn Wilson, former COO of the University of Chicago Health System, provided critical domain expertise during diligence. The round closed in March 2025, the product launched within weeks, and NQS has since grown rapidly. 11 Tribes has made two additional investment tranches, including a recent $750,000 follow-on that effectively constitutes a Series A.

Through The Valley
By Mark Phillips
Every founder has a season they leave out of the story. The stretch where the company almost went under. The years of doubt, failure, and quiet identity crisis that never make it into the profile piece.
Through the Valley is a long-form interview show about those chapters. Host Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, sits down with founders and leaders to talk honestly about what it cost to get here, and who they became on the way through.
New episodes every Wednesday.

Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout.
What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die.
Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born.
In this episode:
• What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair
• The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working
• Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness
• The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time
• How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today
• Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it
• What he would say to himself on the worst night in the valley
Subscribe to Through the Valley wherever you listen. New episodes on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts.
Find Michael at lonelyentrepreneur.com.

Pro Basketball to 5x Founder: A Masterclass in Resilience | Jordan Fliegel
At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement.
He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now.
Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him.
In this episode:
The napkin math that shows exactly when your investors' incentives stop matching yours
Why he ran through Boston in tears to a mentor's office with no appointment
What it feels like to sit in meetings where every good idea you offer undermines your own successor
How he told ten employees the money was gone, and what he had to say to the one he couldn't save
The letter his mentor wrote him, read out loud for the first time
Why he took a company from "we can't pay our bills" to a $48M exit
The Jocko Willink rule he now applies to every piece of bad news

Cancer at 30, and the Company He Built After It | Founder Brandon Aversano, The Alloy Market
In the fall of 2022 Brandon Aversano was 30 years old, away on a trip in California, and found it himself in the middle of the night. Thirty minutes after an ultrasound the chief of urology walked into the room and told him there was a 99% chance it was testicular cancer. His first thought wasn’t about himself. It was how he was going to tell his mom.
Nothing could be known before surgery. Three weeks of sitting with whether it was in one spot or everywhere. His dad had prostate cancer the year before. Brandon had built an identity on competence, distinguished scholar, Deloitte, JetBlue, JP Morgan, and the one thing he suddenly couldn’t do was be the capable one. He went on disability the day after scheduling surgery and had free time for the first time in a decade.
Mark Phillips sits with Brandon on what that season cost and what it built: the medical debt that horrified a father who hated debt, the trip to Jewelers Row with his grandmother’s jewelry where strangers offered twenty cents on the dollar, the 401k he emptied into a company, the $40,000 mobile app his co-founder told him to scrap, and the surgeon who said the book on whether it comes back is already written and he doesn’t get to read the last chapter for five years.
In this episode:
- The 24 hours between finding it himself and hearing the number
- Why telling his parents was harder than hearing the diagnosis
- What three weeks of not knowing does to someone who built his life on competence
- Jewelers Row, twenty cents on the dollar, and the moment Alloy became obvious
- The customer who asked to speak to the founder and had them both crying on the phone
- Learning to control the controllable, and the chapter he doesn’t get to read for five years
- The letter from a friend of eighteen years, and what he’d tell himself on the worst night

Why There's Shame in Getting Sober but None in the Damage | With The Maze Founder Justin Gurland
Justin Gurland arrived at rehab at eleven at night, three thousand miles from everyone he knew. He woke up the next morning in Los Angeles on Super Bowl Sunday, 2008, gave himself the finger in the mirror, and watched the Giants beat the undefeated Patriots. Then the staff turned off the game, walked everyone into a group room, and asked what each of them believed in.
He was twenty-five. He had no community, no sober person anywhere in his life to point at, and no idea what the question meant. What he said was that the Giants had just won and he could hold on to that for now. He describes the moment as meaningless on its face, a football game, a team he wasn't on. It was also the only thing he had.
Mark Phillips sits with Justin eighteen years later, five blocks from The Maze, the members club he opened in the Flatiron where hundreds of New Yorkers pay to belong to a building with no alcohol in it. They talk about the sister who told him she couldn't take it anymore, the letter his father hand-wrote for this episode, the Grateful Dead lyric he keeps returning to, and the question he still can't answer: why the shame attaches to getting sober instead of to the damage.
In this episode:
• Why he says his sister saved his life, and what happens to people who never get that conversation
• The Godfather scene he read a month before everything came apart, and why it stayed with him
• What he actually said when a counselor asked the room about God
• Playing a kids' board game in treatment and feeling his side hurt from laughing for the first time in years
• What his father wrote about Justin's lowest moment, and where his relationship with him sits now
• Why there is shame in getting sober and none in the harm that came before it
• The alcohol-free movement he did not know existed until it was growing in front of him
• What he would say if he could sit with himself on the worst night: take this in, and get to work

Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout.
What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die.
Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born.
In this episode:
• What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair
• The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working
• Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness
• The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time
• How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today
• Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it
• What he would say to himself on the worst night in the valley

Pro Basketball to 5x Founder: A Masterclass in Resilience | Jordan Fliegel
At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement.
He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now.
Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him.

Cancer at 30, and the Company He Built After It | Founder Brandon Aversano, The Alloy Market
In the fall of 2022 Brandon Aversano was 30 years old, away on a trip in California, and found it himself in the middle of the night. Thirty minutes after an ultrasound the chief of urology walked into the room and told him there was a 99% chance it was testicular cancer. His first thought wasn’t about himself. It was how he was going to tell his mom.
Nothing could be known before surgery. Three weeks of sitting with whether it was in one spot or everywhere. His dad had prostate cancer the year before. Brandon had built an identity on competence, distinguished scholar, Deloitte, JetBlue, JP Morgan, and the one thing he suddenly couldn’t do was be the capable one. He went on disability the day after scheduling surgery and had free time for the first time in a decade.
Mark Phillips sits with Brandon on what that season cost and what it built: the medical debt that horrified a father who hated debt, the trip to Jewelers Row with his grandmother’s jewelry where strangers offered twenty cents on the dollar, the 401k he emptied into a company, the $40,000 mobile app his co-founder told him to scrap, and the surgeon who said the book on whether it comes back is already written and he doesn’t get to read the last chapter for five years.
In this episode:
- The 24 hours between finding it himself and hearing the number
- Why telling his parents was harder than hearing the diagnosis
- What three weeks of not knowing does to someone who built his life on competence
- Jewelers Row, twenty cents on the dollar, and the moment Alloy became obvious
- The customer who asked to speak to the founder and had them both crying on the phone
- Learning to control the controllable, and the chapter he doesn’t get to read for five years
- The letter from a friend of eighteen years, and what he’d tell himself on the worst night

Why There's Shame in Getting Sober but None in the Damage | With The Maze Founder Justin Gurland
Justin Gurland arrived at rehab at eleven at night, three thousand miles from everyone he knew. He woke up the next morning in Los Angeles on Super Bowl Sunday, 2008, gave himself the finger in the mirror, and watched the Giants beat the undefeated Patriots. Then the staff turned off the game, walked everyone into a group room, and asked what each of them believed in.
He was twenty-five. He had no community, no sober person anywhere in his life to point at, and no idea what the question meant. What he said was that the Giants had just won and he could hold on to that for now. He describes the moment as meaningless on its face, a football game, a team he wasn't on. It was also the only thing he had.
Mark Phillips sits with Justin eighteen years later, five blocks from The Maze, the members club he opened in the Flatiron where hundreds of New Yorkers pay to belong to a building with no alcohol in it. They talk about the sister who told him she couldn't take it anymore, the letter his father hand-wrote for this episode, the Grateful Dead lyric he keeps returning to, and the question he still can't answer: why the shame attaches to getting sober instead of to the damage.
In this episode:
• Why he says his sister saved his life, and what happens to people who never get that conversation
• The Godfather scene he read a month before everything came apart, and why it stayed with him
• What he actually said when a counselor asked the room about God
• Playing a kids' board game in treatment and feeling his side hurt from laughing for the first time in years
• What his father wrote about Justin's lowest moment, and where his relationship with him sits now
• Why there is shame in getting sober and none in the harm that came before it
• The alcohol-free movement he did not know existed until it was growing in front of him
• What he would say if he could sit with himself on the worst night: take this in, and get to work

Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout.
What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die.
Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born.
In this episode:
• What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair
• The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working
• Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness
• The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time
• How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today
• Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it
• What he would say to himself on the worst night in the valley
Subscribe to Through the Valley wherever you listen. New episodes on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts.
Find Michael at lonelyentrepreneur.com.

Pro Basketball to 5x Founder: A Masterclass in Resilience | Jordan Fliegel
At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement.
He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now.
Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him.
In this episode:
The napkin math that shows exactly when your investors' incentives stop matching yours
Why he ran through Boston in tears to a mentor's office with no appointment
What it feels like to sit in meetings where every good idea you offer undermines your own successor
How he told ten employees the money was gone, and what he had to say to the one he couldn't save
The letter his mentor wrote him, read out loud for the first time
Why he took a company from "we can't pay our bills" to a $48M exit
The Jocko Willink rule he now applies to every piece of bad news

In this first episode of Through the Valley, Jason talks with Mark Phillips about the night he collapsed on his apartment floor, the "cold war" he entered with God, and how the tools he found in his darkest season became the foundation of a coaching firm that now serves some of the most influential leaders on Earth.
They cover why blame keeps you stuck, why self-pity is a drug, the difference between psychological safety and psychological strength, and why community is the closest thing to a bulletproof vest a founder can wear.
Through the Valley is hosted by Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, and explores the seasons of loss, failure, and doubt behind remarkable careers.

Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout.
What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die.
Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born.
In this episode:
• What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair
• The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working
• Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness
• The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time
• How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today
• Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it

Pro Basketball to 5x Founder: A Masterclass in Resilience | Jordan Fliegel
At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement.
He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now.
Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him.

Thirty minutes after an ultrasound the chief of urology walked into the room and told him there was a 99% chance it was testicular cancer. His first thought wasn’t about himself.
